                             © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.

       Fix

The Fix option allows you to fix a Line, Arc, or point to a specific location.
After you select the Fix option, you are prompted to select (in the statusbar) the Line or Arc that you
would like to fix to it's current location.
Now you can see the Fix Constraint has been applied.

If a Fix Constraint is applied to an entity, you are just fixing that the entity should be somewhere
along the trajectory of the entity. In the diagram below the black lines are the fixed entities and the
magenta represent the possible locations of the entity. There is no guarantee of length or position
along the magenta line.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
A line with its center point fixed, basically spins about the center and can be on any angle of
rotation. There is no guarantee of length or angle.

A line with its end fixed, will spin about the fixed end point. There is no guarantee of length or
direction.

               Coincidence

The Coincidence option allows you to Constrain a Line or Arcs endpoint to another Line or Arcs
endpoint so that it is coincident (similar to) to the other. To maintain a closed (valid) Shape each
end-point should be Constrained Coincident to the other.

After you select the Coincidence option you are prompted (in the statusbar) to select the first CAD
Object.

                                © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
The status bar now instructs you to select the next CAD Object...The second CAD object selected
is always the one that moves (Shrinks/Stretches) to meet the first CAD object selected.

Now you can see the Coincidence Constraint has been applied. Notice the Lines endpoint, which
was not Coincident to the other Line's endpoint, is now Coincident to the Line's endpoint. And
because we applied the Coincidence Constraint these Line's endpoints will remain Coincident
when the object changes its size.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
              To make it simpler to create and maintain your shapes, Coincidence Constraints are
       automatically applied to the endpoints of Lines and Arcs endpoints where they meet. That
       way, connected Lines and Arcs stay connected when you edit the shape of the object. It will
       seldom be necessary for you to apply them manually.

Valid Coincidence Selection types

How Constraints Are Automatically Applied

If the Auto-Constraints options are enabled in System Preferences, the system automatically applies
2D constraints according to the methods you use to create new geometry. This topic identifies
which constraints will be automatically applied for a variety of creation methods.

Line Automatic Constraints

Tangent (to an arc, circle, ellipse)           Tangent

Perpendicular to Line                          Perpendicular

Parallel to Line at a Distance                 Parallel

Angle to Line

Position, Endpoint, Midpoint, Center point, Origin Coincidence

Constraint Tutorial

This Tutorial assumes you understand the Constraint tools and how each Constraint type is
applied. See the Constraints topic for more information.

Constraints are a method of applying intelligent parametric rules to Parts. If you are shaping a Part
which does not need to ever change size it is unnecessary for you to apply Constraints to it.
However, if you want to control the Parts Shape you will need to utilize Constraints.

Part 1 - Automatic Constraints

The best way to learn Constraints and how they are applied is to see how the system applies
them.

Let's start by editing the shape of a Standard Base Cabinet.

© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
With the Select Tool active let's select the left-most line and take a look at the Constraints tied to it.
There are three Constraints applied to this line. At each end we have Coincidence Constraints which
locks the ends of the lines to the ends of the respective lines that they touch. There is also a
Vertical Constraint which aligns this line Vertically (Aligned with the Y Axis).

We can also see the Side Type assigned to this selected line in the sidebar. The Type can be
changed here.

Next let's select the line representing the back of the Cabinet. There are three Constraints applied
to this line. At each end we have Coincidence Constraints which locks the ends of the lines to the
ends of the respective lines that they touch. There is also an X-Axis Constraint which aligns this line
with the X Axis.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
We can also see the Side Type assigned to this selected line in the sidebar. The Type can be
changed here.

Next let's select the right-most line and take a look at the Constraints tied to it. There are three
Constraints applied to this line. At each end we have Coincidence Constraints which locks the ends
of the lines to the ends of the respective lines that they touch. There is also a Y-Axis Constraint
which aligns this line with the Y Axis.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
We can also see the Side Type assigned to this selected line in the sidebar. The Type can be
changed here.

Next let's select the line representing the front of the Cabinet. There are three Constraints applied
to this line. At each end we have Coincidence Constraints which locks the ends of the lines to the
ends of the respective lines that they touch. There is also an X-Axis Constraint which aligns this line
with the X Axis.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
We can also see the Side Type assigned to this selected line in the sidebar. The Type can be
changed here.

Overview of Orthographic Editing

Editing in the Orthographic Views (the three face figures) represents one of the more powerful
features of CABINET VISION. Editing at this level typically allows adding unique Parts to your
Assembly and, if necessary, adding intelligence to that Part. Adding intelligence is the process that
gives an existing or new Part the intelligence to respond to changes in the Assembly size caused
by stretching or other dimension changes you may make. Adding new or unique Parts does not
require that intelligence be given to the Part, as the Part may be correct for its intended purpose
as soon as it is added. Typically, "one of" Assemblies do not require intelligence for the new Part,
where production Assemblies that will exist in any of a number of sizes will require intelligence.
New Parts, Part shaping, Part overrides are all possibilities of this form of editing.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
There are three views available for editing in the Orthographic level. These views are sometimes
referred to as the Smiley Face Views. The face icon represents the view of the Assembly that is
available in that view. The three views are shown below. The graphic on the button represents a
head that presents the Face, Top, and End (Profile) view of the head. The orientation of the
graphic reflects the orientation of the view it presents.

Which view you choose to use when editing is more a matter of choosing the view that allows the
best access to the Part or area in question. Any editing done in any of the views above will appear
in the other views if that view allows viewing the edited Part.
Example: If a Shelf's depth is changed, that change would not be visible in the face view, but
would be visible in the top and cross section view.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Adding an Object at the Assembly Level

While in any of the Orthographic Views, you may add a Part from your Object Catalog in the same
manner as Objects are added from the Floor Plan or Elevation Views.

While in one of the Orthographic views (End Ortho view pictured above), click the Objects button
in the sidebar.
The Object library will appear in the sidebar. Simply select the objects that you want to add and
then drag them out into the right side of the screen. Use the position and placement fields in the
sidebar to place the object in the correct location.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.

    you want to add and click Next.

    Library Part.

Perform a Backup

How do I back up my CABINET VISION files?

In Windows 10 or 11 click the Start button or press  then select All Apps and scroll to the

CABINET VISION 2025 Group and run Backup CV 2025 Settings after making any significant changes

to your Material Manager, Material Schedules, Construction Methods, etc. in order to have a

backup of your standards should you need them.

              In previous versions of Windows go to Start | All Programs | CABINET VISION 2025

Transfer My Layer Schedules to another CABINET VISION User

Do Layers get set up in a file that can be copied and pasted to another computer?
Yes, the file is called Default.DAT and is stored in the following location:
C:\ProgramData\Hexagon\CABINET VISION\CV 2025

Transferring Your Standards

      This Topic assumes you are familiar with File Management in the Windows Operating
System.

Follow these instructions to transfer files into CABINET VISION Version 2025 from previous
versions or different computers.

The local hard drive is being referred to as "C" since that is the most common drive designation,
however, it simply represents the drive where CABINET VISION has been installed. If CABINET
VISION has been installed on a different drive on your computer, then that is the one you will use.

© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
This topic describes the procedures for a standalone computer, but it will be the same if you are
using a network server.

Step 1:

Open the Backup Utility. From the CABINET VISION Main Screen, click Utilities and then Backup
Utility.

Step 2:

At a minimum you should "Include" what is in the "Include" area in the illustration below.

Click Save.

             © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
When the backup utility is finished running you must close CABINET VISION.

Step 3:

This creates a folder that contains each of these selected files plus a zipped file called
"backup.zip" which contains all the files in a compressed format. This new folder will be labeled
with today's date and time and will be placed within the Automatic Backups folder. This folder is
located on your hard drive under the Planit or the Cabinet Vision \Solid 8.0, 9.0, 10.0, etc... folder.
If you have 3.5 or older, it will be in the Cabinet Vision \ Solid folder.

Now we need to transfer this newly created backup folder to the Automatic Backups folder within
CABINET VISION Version 2024. If both versions of CABINET VISION are on the same computer,
simply copy and paste this folder from the older Automatic Backups folder to the following folder:

C:\ProgramData\Hexagon\CABINET VISION\Common 2025\Automatic Backups\

If you are transferring these files from one computer to another, simply copy and paste this backup
folder to a USB memory stick or whatever method of transfer you prefer, then copy and paste it to
the folder above on the new computer.

              At this point, make sure that CABINET VISION Version 2025 is closed.

Now that the new folder has been copied to the C:\ProgramData\Hexagon\CABINET VISION\
Common 2025\Automatic Backups folder, follow these steps:

1. In Windows 10 or 11 click the Start button or press  then select All Apps and scroll to the

CABINET VISION 2025 Group and run Restore CV 2025 Settings.

2. The following screen will appear:

© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
3. The screen that pops up shows the available Backup folders on the left and the Files within
    each folder on the right.

4. Make sure you have the folder you just transferred highlighted on the left.
5. Now check which (or all) files you want to restore (transfer) on the right.
6. Click OK

This will copy the selected files into the appropriate Database folder and run the appropriate
update routine. Once the update routine has finished running, CABINET VISION is now ready for

Drawer Box 101

Drawer Box setup begins with the Drawer Guide clearances that are set in the Material Manager.

1. On the Clearance Tab of the Drawer Guide Material, the Side Clearance affects the width of the
    Drawer Box. Also in that area, the Minimum Below Box and Minimum Above Box Clearances
    affect the height of the Drawer Box.

2. The next area that will have an effect on the Drawer Box Size is the Assembly Construction Method.
    There are at least three areas in the Assembly Construction Method that will affect the Drawer
    Box Size. Those areas are:

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
A. In the Assembly Construction Method Branch "Line Boring," there is a setting for Positioning
    Guides on System Holes that will affect the size of Drawer Boxes. The choices for this
    setting are to either restrict Guides to System Holes, or Bore Additional Holes. If you select
    "Restrict Guides to System Holes," then the clearance settings will be a minimum setting
    and the Drawer Box will be made even smaller until the Guide Holes line up with System
    Holes.

B. In the Assembly Construction Method Branch "Line Boring," there is a setting for Aligning
    Horizontal Reveals on System Holes that will affect the size of Drawer Boxes. The choices
    for this setting are to either restrict Face Heights System Holes, or Allow Face Heights to be
    Any Size. If you select "Restrict Face Heights to System Holes," then the Top Drawer Face
    Height setting (Std #165 shown below) will be a minimum setting and the Drawer Front will
    be made larger until the Face Size lines up with System Holes.

                                                               © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
C. Another setting in the Assembly Construction Method that affects the Drawer Box Size is
     the Mid Rail Placement setting in a Face Frame Style Construction Method. This Mid Rail
     Placement setting will create the Top Drawer opening size which is used in conjunction with
     the Drawer Guide Clearance settings to give you the Drawer Box Size.

                                                                © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
3. The next area of CABINET VISION that will affect the Drawer Box is the Drawer Box Material
    Schedule.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
4. Next, the Drawer Box - Roll Out area of the Assembly Manager is the area where the Drawer Box
    Construction is set up. In this area, you should enter the sizing and positioning information for
    the Parts of the Drawer Boxes. This will have no affect on the overall size of the Drawer Box
    but will determine how the Parts of the Drawer Box are sized and join together.

               In the General Object the "Drawer Box Height Specification (Standard #1)" standard, you can
               restrict the Height and Depth of your Drawer Boxes to specified sizes. If you choose to
               use this option, you will force the Drawer Box to be the largest listed size for the space
               available in an Opening.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
5. The last area that has an effect on the Drawer Box size is the Section Editor. When you are inside
    a CABINET VISION Job, the Section Editor would be the place that you would make changes
    that influence the size of a Drawer Box. Changes to the size of the Drawer Opening will
    obviously influence the height of the Drawer Box.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
In the Section Editor, if you Right-Click on the Drawer and click Properties, the Drawer
Properties window will open. There is a Drawer Box tab in the Drawer Properties window
where you can select a different Drawer Box Construction Method, Drawer Box Material, or
Drawer Guide Type. These changes will allow you to have individually adjusted Drawer
Boxes that have different construction, etc. from other Drawer Boxes in the same job or even
within the same Assembly.

                                                         © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Object Tree Settings

In the Object Tree, the Drawer Box settings will be found under the DWR_OPEN. The main
parameters for the Drawer Box Size are the BOXW, BOXH, and BOXD.
BOXD = Depth of Drawer Box
BOXH = Height of Drawer Box
BOXW = Width of Drawer Box

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Drawer Box Sizing
Drawer Set-Up

Setting-up CABINET VISION to produce a Drawer Box with the desired finished dimension
(Drawer Box set-up) and setting-up the individual Drawer Box Part sizes (Drawer Part set-up) are
two separate processes.

Drawer Box Set-Up

Each Drawer Box has a finished overall dimension, a width, height, and depth. We will begin by
setting CABINET VISION to produce the correct width.

WIDTH

The width of a Drawer Box can be expressed as follows:
        Opening - Drawer Guide = Drawer Box Width

CABINET VISION will know the opening, here opening refers to the Case Opening where the
Drawer will reside, from information you provide about your Assembly (Cabinet or Closet)
Construction and Materials. CABINET VISION will determine the value to subtract from this
opening to arrive at the Drawer Box width from information you provide in the Material Manager
for the Drawer Guide. If you look at this screen, you will find the Side Clearance (for each side).

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Lets assume you entered a value of ½ inch (.5 in.) as a property of the Drawer Guide you wish to
use. Further assume that your Case had a clear opening of 21 inches. If you select your Drawer
Guide, the value you have entered for the clearance is substituted (times 2). The formula we used
above now looks like this:

        21 inch opening - (1/2 x 2 or 1) = 20 inch wide Drawer Box.

Many Drawer Guides work better if there is slightly more than ½ inch allowed for each side, and
this is permissible, 9/16 works as well, and would result in a drawer box of 19 7/8 inches wide in
our above formula. Remember, you can have many Drawer Guides in the Material Manager, and,
even repeat the same guide when you desire a larger side clearance.

HEIGHT

It is common for Assemblies to have Drawer Boxes that differ in height depending on Drawer
location. Two possibilities exist to allow these different heights. CABINET VISION may be setup to
produce Drawer Box heights of a pre-selected size, an example would be heights of 10, 8, 6, 4,
2.5 inches. By selecting the option to use standard size Drawer heights, your heights will be limited to
one of the pre-selected sizes according to the available clearance and the properties of the Drawer
Guide you use.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Also, in the Material Manager Clearance tab, you will find two places to input a value that relates
to the clearance that you want to have for your Drawer from any obstruction above or below the
Drawer. These are the "Minimum Below Box and Minimum Above Box" and refer the dimension
from the top of the Drawer Box to the above obstruction, and the bottom of the Drawer Box to the
obstruction below.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Assume you had entered as "Minimum Below Box" .25 inch, and .75 as the "Minimum Above
Box".
The formula would look like this:
Clear vertical opening - top clearance - bottom clearance = drawer height.
Therefore, if we had a clear vertical opening of 6 inches, and a clearance above and clearance
below value that totaled 1 inch, our overall Drawer height would be 5 inches. If we had set up
Solid to use the pre-selected sizes listed above, the 4 inch side would have been selected
because it would be the first one, going from largest to smallest, to fit. Setting up this method will
be covered later.
This is somewhat simplified as other factors enter into the equation that relate to obstructions. In a
Face Frame Cabinet it is simple to see that the face frame opening provides both the clear vertical
dimension and the upper and lower obstruction. Therefore, the values you selected for the upper
and lower clearance are simply subtracted, and the size is determined. Here is an example of
Face Frame.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Drawer Box height Sizing

Frameless/European type construction is not as simple. Many builders choose to put a Drawer
Stretcher below the top Drawer in a Frameless Cabinet. The Drawer face overlays this stretcher by
approximately 3/8 inch, this may vary but is sufficient for the discussion.
When all this is factored into a Drawer height. Our formula for the height of the top Drawer Box
height is more complex:
Drawer face - overlay at Top/Top Stretcher (which is the thickness of the Top/Top Stretcher less the
reveal) - overlay at the Drawer Stretcher - top clearance -"Min Bottom" = Drawer Box height.
Let's assume a ¼ inch top reveal or an overlay of ½"(B), and no reveal at the stretcher so the
overlay is 3/8 inch (C). Further, let's keep the ¾" upper clearance,(D) and the ¼" bottom
clearance (E). And finally, a 6 inch drawer face (A).

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Applying math to the above.
6" (drawer face) - (B or ½) -(D or ¾) - (E or ¼) - (C or 3/8) =
(6 - 1 7/8) or 4 1/8 inch. Now, if you have not selected the standard Drawer height option (we'll
cover this selection in a minute), you would see a Drawer Box height of 4 1/8 inch.
If you go to the Drawer Box - Roll Out area of the Assembly Manager General Object the "Drawer Box
Height Specification (Standard #1)" and select Standard Heights and then continue (Next) to the Drawer
Box Standard Heights (Standard #2) option to enter the available Drawer heights. It is very
important that you enter your heights from the largest at the top, to the smallest. Do Not skip
boxes and place your smallest size in the last box. By selecting this option, you will receive the
first size that fits, from largest to smallest. That is to say, if you have 4 5/8 clear, and choices of
10", 8", 6", 4", 3", and 2, you will receive the 4 inch side. If you really wanted the 3" side here, you
will have to return to the Material Manager, Drawer Guide tab, and add to the clearances so that
the 4 inch side will be too large. Also, in the event that NONE of the sizes you have entered for
your standard heights fit, in other words, they are all too big, CABINET VISION will select a
Drawer height in the same way it would if the "Standard Heights" option were not checked.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Had you selected the Standard Heights, the height would have selected the 4 inch side, as it is the
first one to fit from the above example.

There is a final consideration in the sizing of the Drawer Box heights. If you choose to mount the
Drawer Guides in system holes as opposed to drilling new holes for guide mounting, the process
will work as described above, however, it will continue to reduce the Drawer Box Height until it
finds a system hole to mount to. This may result in Drawer heights shorter than desired. See
Assembly Manager Line Boring for more information.

Length (Depth) of the Drawer Box

If you go to the Drawer Box - Roll Out area of the Assembly Manager General Object the "Drawer Box
Depth Type (Standard #6)" and select Standard Depths and then continue (Next) to the Drawer Box
Standard Depths (Standard #7) option to enter the available Drawer depths. It is very important
that you enter your depths from the longest to shortest. Do Not skip boxes and place your shortest
size in the last box. By selecting this option, you will receive the first size that fits, from longest to
shortest. Also, the dimension you enter for Drawer Box Depth Clearance (Standard #5) refers to the area
between the back of the Drawer Box, and the inside face of the Unfinished Back.

Creating A Dovetail Toolset

From the CV opening screen go to the ribbon option Main | Tool.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Click the "Create New Tool" tool in the toolbar.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Give your Dovetail Tool Set a name and select Dovetail Tool Set as the type.

Next select your new Dovetail Tool Set from the Tool list and fill in the Properties for your Dovetail
Tool Set.

Dovetail Tool Set Properties
General

 Machine - Select the Machine to assign this Tool to. Use the Any selection if this Tool is
   available for all Machines.

 Name - Enter a Name to identify the Tool. The name you give is for your reference only. In
   some posts the tool name will appear in a comment in the g-code next to the tool change.

 Tool Number - Critical for all tools except drills in a gang drill head. This is the ID that Intelli-
   CAM will use to match the Tool to the Machine in the Machine Catalog to the actual Tool on the
   Machine. For drills used in a gang drill head this value is ignored.

 Height Offset ID - This is typically the same value as the tool number or the tool number + 100.
   This number refers to a preset value on the controller that defines the distance from the tip of
   the tool to the top of the spoil board or top of the Material. This is a value set by the CNC
   operator In mathematics and in programming and computer applications, a symbol or other
   character indicating an operation that acts on one or more elements. You can use the following
   four operators in standard calculations: / divide * multiply - subtract + add. It references the
   different heights of the tools above the work surface (In some posts this value is ignored).

 Tool ID - This is a unique ID Number assigned by the S2M CENTER. This value can be called
   from within your design package to assign a specific Tool to a specific Operation. For Example,
   within CABINET VISION, in a User Created Standard you can use the Parameter ToolID equal
   to the Tools Tool ID number to make an assignment.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Tool Size

              Items preceded by a letter designation reference the area noted with that letter in the
       preview area.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Diameter - The S2M CENTER will use this size to match tools to operations.
 Work Depth - This field is used to Display the Graphic for tools. It holds no other importance.
 (A) Bottom Radius
 (B) Max Width
 (C) Top Radius
 (D) Min Width
 (E) Y Pos at Min Width

Dovetail Male Operations

 (F) Rabbet Depth
 (F) Rabbet Tool
 (G) Male Outline Tool

Dovetail Female Operations

 (H) Pocket Width
 (I) Pocket Depth
 (H) Pocket Tool

                   © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 (J) Plunge Depth
 (K) Cut Depth
 (L) Cut Adjustment

               By default the Pocket created is an exact match to the Tool Defined (A, B, C, D, E).
               This option allows you to make a Pocket the is Wider than the Tool in order to perform
               more decorative "wide" dovetails.
 (L) Tail Width Extension
               This option allows you to extend the Width of the pocket to adjust fit.

Nesting

 Nested Part Clearance - Establishes the Part Clearance necessary on the edges of the Part
   where the Dovetail Operation is performed.

Movement

 Rotate Clockwise - This field in addition to the Material field "Climb Cut" will determine the Tool
   path direction. Think of the router bit as a wheel. If the path the wheel is following is the same
   direction, as a wheel would follow if rotated that direction, it is a "Climb Cut" otherwise, it is a
   "Conventional Cut". An inside cut will always be in the opposite direction of an outside cut. A
   "Conventional Cut" will always be in the opposite direction of a "Climb Cut". A simple rule is: If
   the Material is set for a "Climb Cut" an outside pass would be in the same direction of Tool
   rotation. Here is a chart to keep straight all the options: Remember the analogy to the wheel
   that will help keep the matter, including inside, outside, etc... straight.

   Tool Rotation                     Material Climb Cut        Outside
                   Inside (Dado)                                 CCW
     Clockwise                                                    CW
Counter-Clockwise         CW
                        CCW

                   © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Feed Rate

 Feed Rate - This determines how fast the Machine will try to move the Tool through the
   Material. This is often a difficult field to find values for since we lack a standard for feed rate.
    The value represents Inches per minute, or MM per Minute. This can be even further confusing
   since some posts expect a unit but then convert the unit in the post. For example the MultiCAM
   post expects Inches Per Minute but converts the final output to Inches per Second. In addition
   the material will have an effect on the final feed rate. When testing take into account the % feed
   rate property in the Material Catalog.

 Descent Rate - This will have the same unit of measurement as feed rate.
 Spindle Speed - This is the speed at which the tool will spin. The unit is almost always RPM -

   Rotations per minute. Setting a value of 0 here will usually cause an error in the G-Code. A
   valid range would be about 4000 to 24000. It would depend on the Machine and Tool's
   recommended specifications. Some Machines will ignore this number and use a preset number
   for a Tool.

Add Shelf Pins to My Job
I want to add shelf pins to all of my adjustable shelves and have them show up on my Assembly
Sheets and Material Summaries. How do I do this?
1. From the CABINET VISION System Level go to the Part Manager.
2. Click on the Pulls group in the sidebar.
3. Click on the New option in the ribbon and Name it SHFPN.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
4. For Description type in Shelf Pin.

5. Click Close to leave the Parts Manager.

6. Go to the Material Manager.

7. Go to the Pull Category or whatever Category you want to use to store the Shelf Pin.

8. Create a new Miscellaneous Material and name it Shelf Pin (Or whatever name/part number
    you use).

9. Return to the opening screen and go to Material Schedules | Pulls.

10. Attach the Shelf Pin Material to the Shelf Pin item in the Pulls Schedules you use.

11. Close back out to the opening screen.

Now you can write a User Created Standard to add the Shelf Pin to all of your Adjustable Shelves.
Below is the text to utilize in your UCS:

;Links 4 Shelf Pins to Each                 Adjustable  Shelf
  For Each AS Part
   Dim SHFPN as New Pull
   SHFPN.Visible = False
   SHFPN.DX = .125
   SHFPN.DY = .125
   SHFPN.X = 0
   SHFPN.Y = 0
   SHFPN.Z = 0
   SHFPN.AX = 0
   SHFPN.AY = 0
   SHFPN.AZ = 0
   SHFPN.QTY = 4

12. Now go to a new Job and Place a Cabinet on a Wall.

When you print your Assembly Sheet for that Cabinet, look in the Hardware Section and you will see
your Shelf Pin hardware listed.

Create a Door Only Job

Part 1: Creating the Door Only Object

1. Start a new Job using a Frameless Construction Method.

5. Click "Yes" to rebuild the Cabinet back to its Construction Method defaults.

6. Click on the Face and change it to a Door and change the Hinge to "None."

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
7. Go to the Section Editor option Modifications | Hide Parts. Check the boxes as shown below then
    click OK:

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.

 Part 2: Creating the Door Only Job

 1. Start a new Job and select the Doors for each type of Cabinet that you wish to use (in other
      words, select Door & Drawer Styles for Base Cabinets and a Door Style for the Wall Cabinets).
      Also make sure that you set up your Maximum Door size under the Layout tab of Job
      Properties to be a fairly large number (such as 50 inches or larger).

 2. Go directly to the Reports View and click the Order Entry button on the sidebar.

 3. Once in the Order Entry area, simply select the Catalog where your Doors are saved and drag
      it on to the page. This will create a line on the sheet with the dimensions of this Door. You may
      click on the Width and Height and change them to the desired dimensions. You may also
      change the Quantity of a particular line item.

 4. Continue to drag and drop Doors out of your Catalog until you have all of the Doors that are
      needed for the Job.

 5. You can now generate Door Lists and CNC output for them.

  Create Wainscoting

 Step #1
 In the Assembly Manager:

 1. Setup a new or copy an existing Assembly Construction Method that will produce the Door
      Frame parts in the widths and joint configuration that you need.

 2. Use a Mortise & Tenon Connection in the Connection | Top Rail Branch so your cut list will indicate
      correct lengths for stiles and rails. (Allows for coping)

 3. Note any differences in the Toe, as you may want this panel to go to the floor.
 4. Save this Construction Method with a unique name (Wainscot Method).

 Step #2
 In the Door Manager:

 1. Create a new Door with no stiles and rails.
 2. Set the Panel Type to be a Raised Panel.

                                                                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
3. Save the Door with a unique name (Wainscot Panel).

Step #3
In the Material Manager:

1. Create a new Hinge, call it "nohinge"
2. Set it to have a Vertical and Horizontal Offset, use a value like .375" so the Panel will Mortise

    into the Frame.
3. Give it an inset of 3/4".

Step #4
In the Material Schedule Manager:

1. Go to Hinges, create a new Hinge Schedule, call it Wainscot, and use the "nohinge" Hinge for
    this Schedule.

Step #5
In the Material Schedule Manager:

If you do not have the shipping "No Pulls/Knobs" Pull Material Schedule do the following:
1. Go to Pulls, create a new Pull Schedule, call it Wainscot, and use the "MATERIAL NOT

    ASSIGNED" Pull for this Schedule.

Step #6
Set the Job Properties:

1. Start a new Job.
2. Choose anything but the "nopulls" Pull Schedule. (Job Properties/Cabinet/Hardware)
3. Choose anything but the "nohinge" Hinge Schedule. (Job properties/Cabinet/Hardware)
4. Choose anything but the "Wainscot" Door Style. (Job Properties/Cabinet/Doors)
5. Choose anything but the "Wainscot" Construction Method. (Job Properties/Cabinet/

    Construction)
6. We will establish an Override later for each of these selections.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Step #7

Create the Assembly:

1. Place a Base Assembly (you will need to go through all of the following steps again to create
    an Upper Wainscot panel if necessary) on a Wall and then take it to the Assembly Level,
    Section View.

2. At the Section View, choose Modifications | Hide Parts; Hide all Parts except the Door and Frame
    Parts.

3. Go to the Properties Tab, select Construction and change it to Wainscot.
4. Select the Doors Tab and change the door style to Wainscot Panel.
5. Select the Hardware Tab and change the Pulls and Hinges schedules each to Wainscot.
6. All of these choices place overrides on the Assembly. This in effect locks the Construction for

    this object to Wainscot Method, as well as locking overrides on the doors, hinges, and pulls.
    This is beneficial because when we save this assembly to a Catalog it will always have these
    options selected whether the Room it is placed in matches them or not.
7. Section the assembly as necessary and confirm by looking at all other views that this assembly
    is correct.

Step #8

    will be).

5. Name the Subassembly (Wainscot).
6. Go to Advanced/Preserve.
7. Make sure that all of these are checked: Pull Material, Hinge Material, Assembly Construction,

    Door/Applied End Door Style.
8. Click on OK, and then OK again to save the Assembly.

Import 3D DXF's into CABINET VISION

What is a DXF and Why Would I Use It?

DXF stands for Drawing Exchange Format. This drawing format is used with many CAD
(Computer Aided Design) programs. It allows drawings, or objects, rendered in one CAD program
to be imported and used in another CAD program. DXF files done in AutoCAD DXF format can be
imported into CABINET VISION and saved in your object libraries for use in your designs. For
example, you have a DXF of a fireplace mantel that you would like to use in CABINET VISION.
CABINET VISION will import AutoCAD Release 12, 13, and 14 DXF's. Most other CAD and
modeling programs should work just fine as long as they generate polygon based DXF models.
Any non-polygon information within the file (lines, arcs, text, blocks, etc...) is ignored. While there
haven't been any reported problems so far, AutoCAD R14 does have the option to export Release
12 and 13 DXF's.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Rules for creating the DXF's

      How the Solid is described

       The main compatibility problem with importing DXF's into CABINET VISION is that the DXF
       file specification has several ways to describe polygon-based models.

       Polyface Mesh

       This object type defines a group of polygons as a single object. This kind of polygon model
       can be easily imported to CABINET VISION.

       3D Face

       This defines each polygon as a separate object. These import into CABINET VISION as
       well.

       3D Mesh

       Similar, but internally very different, to Polyface Meshes, this type of polygon object can't be
       directly imported into CABINET VISION. Fortunately, most DXF models exported out of other
       modeling programs usually produce either Polyface Mesh or 3D Face models. The one huge
       exception to this is AutoCAD itself: most of its polygon modeling tools creates 3D Mesh
       objects. In AutoCAD, it is possible to convert 3D Mesh objects to 3D Face by using the
       "Explode" command.

      Materials

       The other major compatibility issue is how the DXF file specification indicates what materials
       go on each object. There are three basic ways: by object, by layer, and by color. Models
       that can be imported into CABINET VISION must have unique materials distinguished BY
       LAYER. In the CABINET VISION import dialog, what you are seeing is not individual objects
       but a list of all the layers within the model. Multiple objects that use the same material are on
       the same layer. The majority of existing models distinguish materials by layer, but some use
       the other methods. In fact, it is not uncommon for models to use combinations. For instance,
       a model may have multiple objects on a single layer, each with a different color. CABINET
       VISION would import such a model with all objects being the same material: the color
       information is ignored.

       The 3DS conversion technique described below can be used to convert these to layer based
       models. In step 2, instead of deriving 3DS objects BY LAYER, select BY OBJECT, or BY
       COLOR, as appropriate. It may require some trial and error to find what works best. If all
       else fails, AutoCAD provides many tools for manually editing objects, colors, and layers.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
      Solids

       Another common way to create models in AutoCAD and other programs is as "solids". While
       similar appearing, solid models are very different from polygon models. CABINET VISION
       cannot import AutoCAD or other types of solids directly. Your CAD program must be able to
       convert the solid models into polygon models. In AutoCAD using the 3DS conversion
       technique described below can do this. The 3DS filter automatically converts solids into
       polygons.

3DS Conversion Technique

1. Load DXF or DWG model into AutoCAD.
2. Export model as a 3D Studio (3ds) model. When AutoCAD prompts for it check the box to

    derive 3DS objects BY LAYER, all other settings default.
3. Clear out the current model and re-import the 3DS model back into AutoCAD. When

    prompted, set "Available Materials" to ADD ALL, "Save to Layer" should be set to BY OBJECT,
    and the other settings should be default. The imported model will be imported as a Polyface
    Mesh.
4. Now export it as a DXF.

Importing into CABINET VISION

A DXF can be imported at the Room or Assembly Level. Both are done relatively the same way,
they are just accessed from different area. And if you import at the Job Level it's associating the
object with the Job, where as if you import at the Assembly Level the object is associated with the
Cabinet.

       From the Room or Assembly Level, go to the option Utilities | Import DXF.

Whether you are importing at the Room or Assembly Level, this will bring up the browse window

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
to select your DXF. Click on the object to be imported and select Open.

       You will automatically be taken to the DXF Import window. You will see the DXF displayed in
       the preview window. If this is the file you wish to Import, click on the Type button. You can
       always click the action button to select a different DXF.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Next select the Part Type for this DXF Part and click OK. If you have multiple "Layers" listed
in the Part Type Allocation area you will need to select a Part Type for each "Layer".

                                                         © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
You can now flip or rotate the DXF Part into the preferred orientation by clicking the Flip - X,
Flip - Y, and/or Flip - Z buttons.

                                                         © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
       Select Save and CABINET VISION will place your DXF. You may have to make additional
       adjustments to the imported parts positioning. If you Imported this DXF Part at the Room
       Level you can Save this as a CABINET VISION Object into your Catalog. See the Help file
       Topic on Saving Objects for more information.

Know the Difference Between a UCS and Part Intelligence

Is there a difference between writing a UCS and giving a part intelligence?

Part intelligence is instructions written at the Part level of the Assembly affecting only that
Assembly, while a UCS can be applied to all Assemblies, only specific Assemblies, or all
Assemblies meeting specific conditions which you establish in the UCS. There are benefits to both
methods; the choice of one over the other requires a comprehensive understanding of how both
methods work.

For more information go to the Intelligence Workshop.

Know When to Use a UCS Parameter or Preserves

I need to know a general rule of thumb as to when one should use (or not use) a UCS, Object
Tree Parameters, or just save an Assembly to my Catalog using the Preserve tab (for
Construction Method)?

Here is a simple rule of thumb. If the modification is for one Part (or one Assembly) then typically,
you wouldn't use a UCS.

However, if the modification is going to apply to multiple Assemblies, for example all sink
Cabinets, then write a UCS. The theory behind this rule of thumb is that it is faster to modify one
item without writing a UCS. However it is typically faster to modify two or more items with a UCS.

Make Separate Shared Toe Kick

I construct my Cabinets with a Separate Shared Toe Base. How do I do it?

As with most things in CABINET VISION, there are various ways to accomplish this. The easiest
is to create your toe kick as a separate unit and place it after the Cabinets are designed. After
your design is finished, you know where the Cabinet boxes collide and it makes it a "snap" to drop
in your toe kicks. Here's a quick summary of what you will need to do:

1. Take a Cabinet to the Section Editor and use the Modifications | Hide Parts option to hide all Parts
    except for the Toe Parts.

2. Set the height of the Cabinet to match your toe height.

3. Save the Cabinet back, with Preserve Size checked, into the library with a unique name, for
    example "Kick Box".

4. Now, Setup a new Construction Method for your Cabinets and set it up with no toe kick.

5. Next, drop your default Cabinet that has the auto-fill property enabled into a Room.

6. Right Click on the Cabinet and Select "Save As".

7. Go to Advanced Properties and set the Cabinet to snap to toe height.

8. Save the Cabinet.

Now when you Place or Auto-Fill with Cabinets they will automatically snap to the toe height. After
designing a Job you can then select your Kick Box and it will automatically snap to the floor and fill
the space. Just stretch it to the desired length. You can also right click on the Kick Box and copy
and paste it. Very quick and easy way to get the job done! If you use this method often, I would
also set the Kick Box to appear on my Favorites Bar.

As you know, you can use the Assembly Construction Method to specify when and where you
want sleepers in the construction settings. And you can even use UCS's for the unique cabinet
name "Kick Box" to place your laminate or any other modifications that should only happen to the
TOE KICK!

I am designing a Job that is Frameless. The Shelf Pin Holes on the end panels are not showing
up. What's wrong?

Change the Construction Style to 32mm, instead of Frameless, in the Assembly Manager for your
Construction Method.

Make "The Door Cannot Be Built" Message Go Away

What does the message "Door Cannot Be Built" mean when I use certain Cabinets?

There is a conflict with the Door parts, meaning the Door can not physically be built at the desired
size for the Cabinet.

Go to the Door Catalog, select the Door or Drawer Front used when the message occurs. Check the
Door Associations to see if you've selected a Door for CABINET VISION to switch to when it reaches
a size where that Door can not be built. Also, go to the Construction tab and check the stiles, rails,
and inside edge profiles. Add them up to see if the Door/Drawer can be built at a certain size.
Remember, inside edge profile width's are added to the width of stiles and rails unless the Profile
is designated as Extended.

Remove the Toe Notch from my Knee Drawer Ends

I have noticed that placing a knee drawer next to a Cabinet, even though the toe is "deleted" it
becomes a notched toe on the Unfinished End. How do I keep this from happening?

If you are using a Construction Method that runs the end to the floor for a notched toe it takes
precedence over a Cabinet Editor Modification. The reason for this is that CABINET VISION
evaluates the End condition then builds the Cabinet in place. When it sees the End condition
Finished/Unfinished it looks to the Construction Method for the Job to build the ends, it of course
sees End to Floor and it notches the Toe. When placing a cabinet in a Job using that Construction
Method for the Job you will get a notched toe.

To keep this from happening, from the System Level Assembly Manager copy your Standard
Assembly Construction Method to a new Construction Method called Knee Drawer. In the Knee
Drawer Construction method set the Finished and Unfinished ends Deck/Bottom Connection to
flush with bottom of Deck/Bottom instead of "To Floor". Bring out your Knee Drawer in a new Job.
Go to the Section Editor change the Knee Drawers Construction Method to the Knee Drawer

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Construction Method. Then save it to your Catalog click on Advanced and Preserve the
Construction Method. From now on when inserting the Knee Drawer it will not Notch the Toes.

Remove Toe Kick from Cut List but Not Graphically

I do not want Front Toe on my cut list, however, I do want the toe to display on my elevation and
perspective views. How would I go about accomplishing this?

You could write a UCS similar to:

;Cancels out Toe Dimension

For Each FT Part

 EDX = -DX

The EDX variable is added to the DX value when the part is sent to the cut list. It is a way of
having the size on the cut list different than the graphic. In this case the EDX will cancel out the
DX leaving a result of 0. If either, DX, DY, or DZ of a part is 0 then the part is not output to the cut
list.

              This method will not function for Parts whose Material includes a Model, Models can
       not be re-sized.

OR

You could create a Miscellaneous Material in the Material Manager and give it the correct thickness
and call it "Front Toe". Apply this Material to your Toe Parts in your Material Schedules. Then it has a
length but you will not see it on your cut list.

together by right clicking on them and selecting the desired action.

Setup Multiple Drawer Guide Lengths

How do I properly setup multiple Drawer Guide Length selection?

First off Drawer Guide length is based off of the Drawer Boxes Depth not the Cabinets Depth. The
first step in the process is to verify that Drawer Box Depths are being calculated correctly. If they are
not it does not matter how you setup the Drawer Guide lengths. Once you have verified that the

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Depths of the Drawer Boxes are correct then focus on the Drawer Guide Lengths.
Make sure that the Parent guide is set to the shortest length you would use. Then set each
increment above that down the line.
Parent --- Accuride 12"
>= 14 --- Accuride 14"
>= 16 --- Accuride 16"
>= 18 --- Accuride 18"
>= 20 --- Accuride 20"
>= 22 --- Accuride 22"
>= 24 --- Accuride 24"

              The Greater Than or Equal to references the Drawer Box Depth. A Drawer Box Depth,
       in the above scenario, Greater than or Equal to 14" would utilize the Accuride 14" Drawer
       Guide.
Keep in mind that it uses the Parent if the other conditions are not met, in this case a Drawer Box
depth that is less than 14" would utilize the Parent, in this case Accuride 12". If I had my Parent
setup as Accuride 22" it would place a 22" guide on Drawer Box Depths less than 14". As you can
see setting the Parent wrong can cause problems.
The key here is to verify that the Drawer Box depths are correct first. Then focus on the Guide
Schedules. If you follow these basic "guide" lines you shouldn't have any problems.

Stop Parts from Being Added when I Size a Cabinet

stretchers, and Doors. How can I keep the Cabinet the same when it stretches?

number (ex. 90) to keep CABINET VISION from putting a pair of Doors and mid-rails into Cabinets
as they stretch.

Assign a Specific Outline Tool to a Material

I need to run a specific Outline Tool on a certain Material and the Tool is not my default Outline
Tool. How do I do this?

This can be handled easily via a UCS. Let's say you wanted to use your 3/8 compression bit
which is not your Outline Tool to always cut out your 1/4" Unfinished Backs. The first thing you
need to do is identify the 3/8 Compression Tool's Tool ID Number. The Tool ID# is in a grayed out
field in your Tool Catalog. Once you have this number let's say its 13 then your UCS would look
like this:

;Make the 3/8 Compression the Unfinished Back Outline Tool

For Each UB Part

TOOLID = 13

If your Unfinished Backs, depending on selected Material Schedule, could be also made out of 3/
4" Material that you would want to use your default Outline Tool on. You could add an additional
Material filter to the UCS. First you will need to get the Material ID# for your 1/4" Material from the
Material Manager. Then write your UCS like this:

;Make the 3/8 Compression the Unfinished Back Outline Tool

For Each UB Part

If _M:MatID = 123 Then

 TOOLID = 13

End If

Troubleshoot No Tool Found Errors

Why am I getting this message after I Optimize saying, "No Tool found for dado or bore..."?

For Line Boring:

Make sure the diameter of a Tool in the Tool Catalog is an exact Diameter match for the
Operation. If you defined the Operation in millimeters make sure you also define the Tool in the
Tool Catalog in millimeters and vice versa.

Make sure the Vertical Drill tool in the Tool Catalog is assigned to the Machine you are using in the
S2M CENTER. The safest assignment is N/A which means any Machine defined in the Machine
Catalog can utilize the Tool.

Make sure there is a valid Tool in the Tool Catalog available for this operation.

For Dadoes:

Make sure the width of the Dado is not smaller than the width of the smallest diameter Flat Router
bit in the Tool Catalog.

Make sure the Flat Router bit in the Tool Catalog is assigned to the Machine you are using in the
S2M CENTER. The safest assignment is N/A which means any Machine defined in the Machine
Catalog can utilize the Tool.

Make sure there is a valid Tool in the Tool Catalog available for this operation.

Position a Wall in a Specific Location

How do I place a Peninsula Wall in an exact location within my layout?
There is an easy way to do this in CABINET VISION, using the Snap Points. Snap Points allow
you to place points in exact locations, and then attach Walls, Cabinets or other Objects to the
points.
Snap points can be placed by using the Measure Tools | Snap Marks ribbon option. They can be
placed so they snap to objects, to the grid, other snap points or placed freely without snapping to
anything by changing the Snap Setting Options (the buttons with magnets in the statusbar menu).
Placing the Points:
After choosing Snap Marks. Move the cross hair/cursor to where you want your start point, left
click one time to place the point. Next use the keyboard to tab through the Horizontal and Vertical
position fields in the side of the screen to pace the next point.

Add Lights to My Room for the Proper Effect

We have had trouble lighting 3-D views of rendered drawings. When placing lights to highlight
certain areas of Room we often wash out the color of the Cabinet, Wall, and/or Floor. We have
tried to dim lights but do not get the desired effect. Is there a rule of thumb or basic plan to help us
learn how to place lights correctly?

Here are some helpful tips for setting up lighting:

 Instead of trying to light a Room as it would be in "real" life, imagine that it is instead a stage.
   When the light is red - it is a "spot" light. A "spot" light is a much more intense light and will
   wash out a scene easily. We recommend switching your general lights to "directional" lights
   (blue in color) on the "beam" tab. Use these directional lights to fill the light in the Room and the
   spot light to highlight areas that you want to draw attention to. "Spot" lights also seem to always
   wash out light colored finishes, so stick with "directional" lights in that situation.

 Start by placing only 2 lights - one on the left pointed right, and one on the right pointed left. Set

           © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
   them at about eye level (60" to 65") and vary the angles of each. This will help to create nice
   shadows. Test these until you are happy, then save them in a light schedule.

 Do all of this before you place a lot of "extra fancy" objects such as toasters etc. These will slow
   your rendering time down drastically. If you have a Job you have already done this too - just
   copy it to a new Room and delete the detailed items. You can save the light schedule to use in
   other Rooms and delete the copied Room when you are done.

 The more lights you add the slower the rendering time. So only add a few more lights to draw
   attention or to create an effect - such as light through a window, under counter lighting, or light
   in a glass cabinet.

Hopefully these few tips will help shed some "light" on Rendering.

Align Drawing Scenes

Is there a way to get Scenes to line up with other Scenes on a sheet (besides "eye balling it")?

Yes, you can use the Point or Grid Snap settings to "Snap" the Scenes where you want them.

To use Point Snaps, use the Snap Marks option to place points where you need them, then change
to "Snap to Point" on your Snap settings statusbar button. Now you can "Snap" your Scenes to the
Points you've placed.

To use the Grid Points, right click on the screen to turn your Grid pattern on and to modify the Grid
Snap spacing and Grid spacing, then change to "Snap to Grid" on your Snap settings toolbar
button. Now you can "Snap" your Scenes based on the Grid space settings you've chosen.

Re-sizing Objects and Setting Dimensions

Cabinets and other Objects are saved to your library at default dimensions. Your typical wall
cabinet may be 12 inches deep, therefore, you may choose to have that value as the default
value. This doesn't mean that it must remain 12 inches deep indefinitely, as it can be stretched or
dimensioned to any necessary size, but there must be some default size. You will select this size
and modify it as the need occurs, therefore, select this dimension, as well as other dimensions for
cabinets that represents your most common need, and choose the "set as default" option. This
option sets the Default Height, and the Default Depth of your cabinets. From the Layout level,
select Room | Cabinet | Layout to see your default values.

The following graphic shows a cabinet in plan view, after highlighting it. The dots are used for
sizing or moving the cabinet as explained on the graphic.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Note also the "Clearance" data boxes in the sidebar. These data boxes can be used to place the
Assembly in specific locations along the Wall. The "Clearance" tool references the available area
to the left or right of the Assembly before another object or Wall is encountered. The measurement
is from the object that would interfere to the dot on the side of the Assembly, be it left or right. The
next series references Position. This is similar, except that it references the Assembly position to
the Wall end, regardless of whether there is another object in the way or not. The last series,
Center, references the position of the yellow dot in the center of the Assembly to the Wall ends.
When the two dimensions are equal, the Assembly is in the center of the wall.

Entering data in these data boxes can be done by deleting what is there and entering the new
data, OR, you can add (or subtract) a value to the value already there. For instance, if the Width
box shows an Assembly that is 33 1/16 inches wide, and you wish to reduce it by 5/8 inch, click
your mouse to the right of the 6 in 1/16 (do not highlight the entire dimension). The cursor should
be a blinking straight line to the right of the 33 1/16. Now, enter a "-' (minus sign) and 5/8. Press
enter. CABINET VISION will treat this as a math equation and change the dimension from 33 1/16
to 32 7/16. To add, use the "+" (plus) sign instead of the minus sign. This will work in all of the data

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
boxes on this page.

Overview of Parametric Editing

Parametric editing refers to the addition, deletion, or modification of Parameters as they relate to
objects within CABINET VISION. An example of a Parameter would be the width (DX) of a Part,
the location of a Part (X, Y, or Z), even the material (MatID) of a Part. All of these are necessary to
define the Part or object in order for it to become what it needs to be. When the Parameters are
missing, or do not represent what you need, the solution is to edit the Parameter by adding,
deleting, or modifying it. This is the section where that process is discussed.

Due to the complexity of parametric editing, do not approach the matter with the expectation that
you will understand all there is to learn after working through this group of topics. Parametric
editing is an art that is developed and perfected as you work with it. The more you work with it, the
more you will learn about it's capabilities. The power of these features are truly awesome, as you
will see.

A final word on becoming proficient with these tools. The best teacher is the experience gained
through practice. Mistakes encountered as you work with these tools lead to solutions.

Part and Object Orientation

The presentation of a Part on your screen occurs because CABINET VISION has applied a
mathematical formula that represents information regarding the point of origin of the Part or object,
and the final dimension it requires. The use of the 9 Basic Parameters provides this data.
Understanding how these Parameters respond and thereby position Parts and objects is an
important part of understanding how intelligence is applied to objects.

Assemblies widths align along the X axis, with their height following the Y axis. The depth of an
Assembly follows the Z axis. On the following graphic, note the back, bottom, left corner of the
Assembly as the point of origin and the variables DX, DY, and DZ representing the overall size of
the Assembly.

Standard Part Orientation

All Parts are created equal in Solid. When initially brought into CABINET VISION, they are
orientated in the "standard Part orientation" that is shown on the following graphic.

Notice that the width of a Part follows the X axis (as does an Assembly) the Length follows the Y
axis, and the thickness follows the Z axis.

If this Part were an End Stile, all would be well, as it is orientated correctly for that use. However, it
is necessary to rotate Parts so that they will assume the correct orientation for their intended use.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Assume that the above Part was to be a Bottom Rail, it would need to be rotated from its present
position 90 degrees to the right, to orientate itself as a Bottom Rail would. Because ALL Parts;
Tops, Backs, Ends, etc. enter CABINET VISION following standard Part orientation, most Parts
will have to have a unique rotation applied to it to get it into the correct orientation for it's intended
use.

Rotation that occurs clockwise is a negative rotation, conversely, rotation in a counter clockwise
direction is positive rotation. The two are distinguished by adding a "-" to the negative rotation, and
simply entering the value for the positive rotation (I.E. -90 or 90).

The graphic below represents an End Stile that has been rotated -90 degrees along the Z axis. It
is now correctly orientated as a Bottom Rail.

Notice that the rotation has not changed, the original orientation as far as which axis represents
length, width and thickness. The Y axis will remain the axis of the length of the Part regardless of
the degree or number of times the Part is rotated. Length is always along the "Y" axis, and is
always represented by the DY variable. The same for the other axis involved. This is a very
important point when, at a later time, you will apply intelligence to a Part and use the parameters
of a Part as a parent.

Writing Formulas

Introduction

Formulas are used to provide the intelligence to a Part that needs to respond to changes in an
Assemblies dimensions. Formulas can be used to position a Part within an Assembly so that the
Part remains relative to a pre-selected position. They can also used to provide the Part you have
added to an Assembly with logic so that the Part becomes an integral Part and intelligent to the
changes in the Assembly.

Formulas can also be used to add to the dimension of a Part for cut list purposes, yet have the
Part remain represented graphically in its proper size.

Example: A formula to have a Part appear on the cut list ½ inch larger than the finished size, but
have the Part display correct graphically.

Position References

Position references vary somewhat depending on whether the item being positioned is a Part, an
Assembly, a Wall, or other object. The reference to the Part is as follows:

The 9 Basic Parameters

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
       X = the horizontal axis

       Y = the vertical axis

       Z = the axis perpendicular to X and Y

       DX = the variable representing width

       DY = the variable representing length

       DZ = the variable representing depth or thickness

       AX = the variable representing rotation on the x axis

       AY = the variable representing rotation on the y axis

       AZ = the variable representing rotation on the z axis

These 9 basic parameters define the location and size of all objects within CABINET VISION.
Their use is demonstrated below.

Adding Parts

To add a Part in an Assembly, complete the following steps.

1. From the Assembly Level Face Ortho View, select the Add Part button in the sidebar.

2. Select a Part name from the list on the left. Then press Next. We will use "Board" in the
    example, however, you may use any Part name. You may also add Part names to the
    Part Manager for use here.

3. The next screen is for the Parts Dimension. Change this to the dimensions needed. We will
    leave this alone, for our example as the dimensions are fine for our use.

4. The next screen is how you want the Part Oriented in relationship to the Assembly initially. You
    can rotate the Part any way you want, so this just saves some time by selecting approximately
    how you want the Part to come into the picture.

5. Review the Finish for the Part. If you want to change any one of these, select the Finish Type
    dot. From the right side, pick the appropriate Finish.

6. By selecting Finish, you will now return to the orthographic view with the Part showing next to
    the Assembly.

Positioning Parts

We will now position the Part so it will show properly and have some intelligence when the
Assembly is re-sized.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
If you wish to follow the text below, bring your new Part into the face view of the orthographic
views, and position it "to Front". Leave the dimensions as they are.

The initial placement of this Part ("Board") will be at the bottom, back, left side of the Assembly.

Typically, the Assembly Bottom, Back, and Left End are positioned at X=0, Y=0, and Z=0. The DX,
DY, and DZ values are variables. All Objects have a DX, DY, or DZ value. These variables
represent the dimensions of the Assembly as well as the Part.

The variable DX represents the width of the Assembly, but the value of DX may differ from one
Assembly to another. Because we can change the value of DX, until we determine the actual
width of an Assembly, DX remains a variable. Once an Assembly is placed on the screen and is
sized to 30 inches wide, then and only then does the value of DX = 30.

The same is true for DY, which represents the height of an Assembly. An Assembly with a DY
value of 34 ½ would be 34 ½ inches high. DZ represents the depth of an Assembly.

The Object Tree

The Object Tree represents the hierarchy of a Job or an Assembly. The Object Tree is similar to an
outline of a book. The structure of a book outline gives you major headings (chapter titles), sub-
headings (section titles), and sub-sub-headings (paragraph titles), etc. The Job or Assembly tree
can also be analogous to the outline of a book, and to a tree and its branching structure. Hence
the title "Tree". Each item of a Job occupies a particular place on the tree and its branching
structure similar to the outline described above. If we were to isolate the Assembly, then at the
Assembly Level, the same tree structure applies, but to the local, or Assembly Level.

The Object tree at the Assembly Level is a sidebar tab at the very bottom of the sidebar, select
the Object Tree tab .

Highlight the name of the Assembly that you are viewing, and you'll see information regarding its
size. Our 30"W x 34 ½"H x 24"D Assembly would be referred to in the Object Tree as follows:

       DX = 30(Static)

       DY = 34.5(Static)

       DZ = 24(Static)

       X= represent the starting position of the Assembly along the Wall (from left)

       Y= represents the elevation of the Assembly (from floor)

       Z= represents the distance from the back Wall (if any) if any.

       AX A rotation on the X axis would be listed in degrees here.

AY A rotation on the Y axis would be listed in degrees here.
AZ A rotation on the Z axis would be listed in degrees here.

                Assembly rotation is typically limited to the Y axis, if at all.

Individual Parts can be viewed in outline form by finding them on the Object Tree menu and
highlighting them. When the Part is highlighted, the values represented here are relative to the
Part.

The X, Y, and Z values, with no other letter designation in front of them, represent the location of
the Part on (or In) the Assembly relative to the Assembly.

The "D?" (where "?" represents an X, Y, or Z) values represent the overall dimension of the Part.
The "A?" values represent any angle of rotation that the Part has undergone.

Writing Formulas

Formulas are used to position a Part and to add intelligence to the Part.

From the Assembly Level Face Ortho View bring in a Board, (new Part, Board, etc)

You will see this Board to the left of your Assembly. It will be positioned so that it sits on the
narrow end, and its length (which is along the "Y" Axis) is represented by the variable "DY" on the
object tree. It's width is represented by the variable "DX", and it's thickness, by the variable "DZ".

We are going to position this Part in our Assembly as if it were a Mid Stile. To do this, we need to
give the Part intelligence in the following areas:

1. It's height above the floor (Y + Some value so it sits above the deck).

2. It's position in the middle of the Assembly.

3. It's position at the face of the Assembly.

4. It's relationship in length to the length of the opening it fills.

By providing formulas for these 4 items, we will have given logic to the Part sufficient for it to
respond to Assembly dimension changes and remain in the same relative position.

Height of a Part

To set height of our new Part, or the "Y" position, do the following:

1. From the Assembly Level Face Ortho View, select the Object Tree tab  in the sidebar.
2. Highlight the Part, "Board".

© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
3. From the small window to the right, highlight the "Y" value.
4. Click the Edit button.
5. Click the Equation dot.
6. Click the Add button.
7. Enter a "1" (no quotes though) in the first box. This means "if true".
8. Enter "case.y +4.75" in the second box (again, no quotes). This entry means this. Substitute

    the "Y value of the case, plus 4 ¾ inches" as the value of "Y" for the board.
The board now looks to the case, and finds its "Y" value, and adds 4 ¾ inches to it for its own
value.
Horizontal Position of Part (left to right)
To set our new Part to remain in the center of the Assembly, (the "X" position), do the following:

From the Assembly Level Face Ortho View, select the Object Tree tab in the sidebar.
1. Highlight the Part "Board".
2. From the small window to the right, highlight the "X" value.
3. Click the Edit button.
4. Click the Equation dot.
5. Click the Add button
6. Enter a "1" (no quotes though) in the first box. This means "if true"
7. Enter "case.dx/2 - (board.dx/2)" in the second box (again, no quotes).
This entry means this. Use the full length of the case (dx), divided by 2 which represents the
"center" of the case. Because we are positioning the "X" position of a Part that is 2 ½ inches wide,
( an "X" position of "0" and a DX of 2 ½" for the board), we need to set the center of the board to
the center of the case. The last part of the equation ( - board.dx/2) provides that ½ of the DX of
the board, (or 1.25") will be subtracted from the value returned by case.dx/2 value.
In the case of the 30 inch wide Assembly, the actual math will be as follows
case.dx/2 = 30/2 or 15", minus board.dx/2 =2.5/2 or 1.25
OR

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
15-1.25 = 13.75

If you click the "Test" button it should return "condition returned = TRUE" and "formula returned =
13 3/4".

This was one of the more difficult formulas in that we used ½ the value of the case size, not the 0
value of the case X to get our Part positioned.

We used the DX value of the board instead on using the numeric value to protect against future
changes to the Assembly where the board width might be changed to 3". By using ½ of the DX
value, whatever future width the board assumes, the equation remains valid. No matter how wide
the Assembly becomes, our board will always be in the center.

              Whenever possible, use a variable (DX, DY, or DZ) of a Part rather than the constant
       (the actual dimension of the Part) to modify the position of the Part. That way you add even
       more flexibility to the formulas of the Assembly.

Horizontal Position of Part (front to back)

To set depth of our new part, or the "Z" position, do the following:

1. From the Assembly Level Face Ortho View, select the ribbonbar option Object Tree tab in
    the sidebar.

2. Highlight the Part "Board".

3. From the small window to the right, highlight the "Z" value.

4. Click the Edit button.

5. Click the Equation dot.

6. Click the Add button

7. Enter a "1" (no quotes though) in the first box. This means "if true"

8. Enter "case.dz - board.dz" in the second box (again, no quotes).

This equation provides the following information to CABINET VISION.

"Position the board at the full depth of the case (DZ) minus the Thickness (DZ) of the board. This
assumes a Frameless Cabinet, if the Cabinet had a Face Frame, the "-board.dz" would not be
needed.

Establish Length of Part

To set the length of our new Part, or the "DY", do the following:

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
1. From the Assembly Level Face Ortho View, select the Object Tree tab in the sidebar.
2. Highlight the Part "Board".
3. From the small window to the right, highlight the "DY" value.
4. Click the Edit button.
5. Click the Equation dot.
6. Click the Add button
7. Enter a "1" (no quotes though) in the first box. This means "if true"
8. Enter "case.dy" in the second box (again, no quotes).
This equation provides the following information to CABINET VISION.
"Adjust the length of the board to equal the length of the case." This may be adjusted by adding or
subtracting a value from the result returned by following the equation with a plus or minus sign
and a value. The result of this equation will cause the board to maintain its size relative to the
case.

              When choosing what you want to use as the reference for adding logic, be sure that
       you do not choose something that may change later on. As an example, if you relate a Part
       to the size of a Mid Stile, and later on, you delete the Mid Stile from this Cabinet for a Job,
       the formulas you wrote will be invalid.
Troubleshooting Error Messages
There are three reasons for 95% of the errors returned when writing a formula.
A Part name (or code) has been entered incorrectly or misspelled.
The periods within your "then" statement have been left out, or a comma was entered.
The path to the Part is not correct. For instance looking at the Object Tree, you'll see that the
Adjustable Shelf (code AS) is under the "Interior", not the "Case" Branch. If your statement used
"case.as", to refer to the Adjustable Shelf, an error would be returned. The correct statement
would be "interior.as".
The path is evident by looking at the Object Tree, and looking "Up" to the parent of the Part in
question. It is structured much like a "directory, sub-directory" tree structure.
