Welcome

Adding Intelligence to a Manually Placed Part

Writing formulas is like anything else you want to learn to do. You need to know a few basics and
then you need to practice, practice, and practice some more. You must invest the time to read this
document, and to work through all the sample exercises in the sequence presented. If you will
invest the time and do the exercises, you will learn to write formulas. Writing formulas is actually
fairly simple and very logical.

First you figure out what it is you are trying to do and you write it down, this is your "formula".
Believe it or not, this is the hard part. We know how to do what we want to do; we just have never
had to write it down in a logical way.

Second you trace what you have written down through the Object Tree to get your "code", this is
the easy part.

The ability to write formulas will open an exciting, new world of things you can do with CABINET
VISION.

In order to add intelligence to a manually placed part you are going to need to know a little about
the following subjects:

 The Nine Basic Parameters

 The Reference Point

 Part Orientation

 The Orthographic Views

 The Object Tree

 Formulas

 Tracing the Object Tree

 How to Differentiate between Multiple Parts with the same "Name"

Nine Basic Parameters

Parameters

A parameter is a characteristic or attribute of an object. In CABINET VISION a room is an object,
a cabinet is an object, a part is an object. An example of a parameter would be the length of a
part.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Nine Basic Parameters

There are nine basic parameters. For all practical purposes every object in CABINET VISION will
have the nine basic parameters, although most objects will have more than the nine basic
parameters. The nine basic parameters define the position, size, and rotation, of every object in
CABINET VISION. CABINET VISION allows you to access the parameters for an object, ether by
going to what is called the "Object Tree" or by going to the "Properties" for that object or by writing
a User Created Standard. The nine basic parameters are as follows:

The "Positional" parameters are:

X, Y, and Z these parameters are used to record the position of an object. Changing the position
of an object will change the values stored in one or more of these parameters. See the Positional
Parameters topic for more information.

The "Sizing" parameters are:

DX, DY, and DZ these parameters are used to record the size of an object. Changing the size of
an object will change the values stored in one of more of these parameters. See the Sizing
Parameters topic for more information.

The "Rotational" parameters are:

AX, AY, and AZ these parameters are used to record the rotation of an object. Rotating an object
will change the values stored in one or more of these parameters. See the Rotational Parameters
topic for more information.

Positional Parameters

The "Positional" parameters are: X, Y, and Z, these parameters are used to record the position of
an object, in relation to its parent object, such as an Assembly on a Wall, or a Part in an Assembly.
The Wall would be the parent for the Assembly, and the Assembly would be the parent for the
Part.

X = Left and Right

The left and right position of an object, also called its X position. A positive adjustment will move
the object to the right of its parents "Reference Point", while a negative adjustment will move the
object to the left of its parents "Reference Point". For example if the X position of a Cabinet were
23" (X = 23), we would know that the Cabinet was 23" from the left end of the Wall (toward the
right end of the Wall). See the diagram below.

Y = Up and Down

The up and down position of an object, also called its Y position. A positive adjustment will move
the object up from its parents reference point, while a negative adjustment will move the object
down from it parents reference point. For example if the Y position of a Cabinet were 23" (Y = 23)

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
we would know that the Cabinet was raised 23" off the floor. See the diagram below.
Z = Front to Back (or In and Out)
The front to back position of an object, also called its Z position. A positive adjustment will move
the object forward from its parents reference point, while a negative adjustment will move the
object backward from its parents reference point. For example if the Z position of a Cabinet was
23" (Z = 23) we would know that the Cabinet was 23" away from the face of the Wall. See the
diagram below.
Position References

Sizing Parameters
The "Sizing" parameters are DX, DY, and DZ these parameters are used to size an object. The
letter D in DX, DY, and DZ stands for Dimension. Any time you are doing anything with the
dimensions of a Part the parameter will start with a D.
DX = the width of an object
If the object is a Cabinet then DX is the width of the Cabinet, if the object is a Part then DX is the
width of the Part. The DX measurement is always across the grain of a Part.
DY = the length or the height of an object
If the object is a Cabinet then DY is the height of the Cabinet, if the object is a Part then DY is the
length of the Part. The DY measurement is always with the grain of a Part.
DZ = the thickness or depth of the object
If the object is a Cabinet then DZ is the depth of the Cabinet, if the object is a Part then DZ is the
thickness of the Part. The DZ measurement is always from the "Back" of the Part toward the

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
"Face" of the Part.

                      If the object is a Part, you will most likely never write a formula for its thickness as
               the thickness of a Part is determined by the thickness of the Material the Part is made
               from.
Sizing Parameters For an Assembly
 DX = the width of the Assembly.
 DY = the height of the Assembly.
 DZ = the depth of the Assembly.
Sizing Parameters For a Part
 DX = the width of the Part, across the grain.
 DY = the length of the Part, with the grain.
 DZ = the thickness of the Part.
Rotational Parameters
The "Rotational" parameters are AX, AY, and AZ. These parameters are used to rotate an object.
It is very rare to write a formula to rotate a Part, as once you have the Part in an Assembly and
rotated into the proper position, you normally don't need the angle of rotation to change. However,
it is important to understand how Parts are rotated, because when Parts are rotated it changes the
position of the reference point for the Part.
AX = the angle of rotation around the X-axis
The X-axis of rotation moves a Part around the X-axis in the same fashion as a gymnast swings
around a horizontal bar. Or you could think of it as holding a pencil with the tip pointing to the right
so that the length of the pencil is running left and right. You then roll the pencil with you fingers;
this is rotation in the AX.

AY = the angle of rotation around the Y-axis

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
The Y-axis of rotation moves a Part around the Y-axis in the same fashion as the rope of a tether-
ball swings around a pole. Or you could think of it as holding a pencil with the tip pointing up so
the length of the pencil is running up and down. You then roll the pencil with your fingers; this is
rotation in the AY.

AZ = the angle of rotation around the Z-axis
The Z-axis of rotation moves a part around the Z-axis in the same fashion as a propeller rotates
on an airplane as you face it. Or you could think of it as holding a pencil with the tip pointing at you
so that the length of the pencil is running from front to back. You then roll the pencil with you
fingers; this is rotation in the AZ.

Reference Point
Imagine an Assembly with no Parts in it; it would be an empty box. All you would have is just the
outline of the Assembly. This empty box would have width, height and depth but no Parts. In the
left, bottom, back corner of this empty box is an imaginary point called the "Reference Point". An
Assembly is positioned on a Wall in reference to this point and the reference point of the Wall. All
Parts added to the Assembly will be positioned referenced to this reference point and the
reference point of the Part.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Reference point of an Assembly

The reference point for an Assembly is in the left, bottom, and back corner of the Assembly.

Reference point of a Part

The reference point of a Part is in the left, bottom, and back corner of the Part, when that Part is in
normal orientation, in other words, if the Part has not been rotated.

Normal Orientation

Part in Normal Orientation

The following graphic shows a Part in what is called "Normal Orientation" (front orientation). All
Parts added to an Assembly, by CABINET VISION, will come into the Assembly in "Normal
Orientation" (front orientation). The length of the Part will be running up and down. The width of
the Part will be running left and right. The thickness of the Part will be running from back to front.
The front (or face) of the Part will be facing you and the top of the Part will be at the top. The
"Reference Point" for a Part in normal orientation is the left, bottom, and back corner of the Part. A
rail, a stile, a left end, a right end, a door, a drawer box bottom, all Parts are built by CABINET
VISION, starting with the same orientation and then are moved and rotated into place.

                      The reference point will always be on the backside of whatever Material a Part is
               made from. The reference point will never be on the face side of the Material a Part is

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
               made from. This will make more sense later.

The following diagram is an example of a rail and how the orientation and position differs from
normal orientation and position once it is placed in an Assembly.

Notice how the X (left and right) and the Y (up and down) and the Z (front to back) are different;
reflecting the rails new position in the Assembly. Also notice that the Part has been rotated -90
degrees on the AZ to lie down flat clockwise.
Positive (+) and Negative (-)
With the AX, AY, & AZ parameters, if you are facing the reference point, a positive number will
rotate the object counter clockwise and a negative number will rotate the object clockwise.
Facing the Reference Point

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
It is important to know how to face the reference point so you will know if you need to enter a
positive amount or negative amount to cause the Part to rotate in the correct direction.

Notice the graphic above, notice also the X, Y, and Z-axis; say you wanted to rotate this Part
toward you so that the face of the Part was facing down. It would be the X-axis that would act like
a hinge, so that the Part could lay face down. To know if we needed to enter a positive amount, or
a negative amount, to lay this Part face down. We would have to face the reference point. So we
must look down the X-axis toward the "Reference point". In order to look down the X-axis toward
the "Reference Point" we will have to look at the Part from a right side view. Or visualize that we
are looking at the Part from a right side view. Looking at it this way we would have to enter a
positive amount for the Part to lay face down, or a negative amount if we wanted the Part to lay
face up.

Ortho View

You can look at the Part in a right side view by going to what is called an "Ortho" view.

Right click on an Assembly and select "Edit". Once you are at the Assembly Level click on the right
side "Ortho" view, using the "View" buttons across the top of your screen. The views are as
follows: Face View, Top View, and Right Side View.

Say you wanted to tip this Part to the right so that the top of this Part faced to the right. It would be
the Z-axis that would act like a hinge, so that the Part could rotate to the right. To know if we
needed to enter a positive amount, or a negative amount, we would have to face the reference
point. So we must look down the Z-axis toward the "Reference point". In order to look down the Z-
axis toward the "Reference Point" we will have to look at the Part from a front view. Or visualize
that we are looking at the Part from a front view. Looking at it this way we would have to enter a

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
negatives amount for the Part to tip to the right or a positive amount if we wanted the Part to tip to
the left.

Say you wanted to rotate this Part so that the face of the Part was facing to the left. It would be the
Y-axis that would act like a hinge, so that the Part could face toward the left. To know if we needed
to enter a positive amount, or a negative amount, we would have to face the reference point. So
we must look down the Y-axis toward the "Reference point". In order to look down the Y-axis
toward the "Reference Point" we will have to look at the Part from a top view. Or visualize that we
are looking at the Part from a top view. Looking at it this way we would have to enter a negative
amount for the Part to turn to the left or a positive amount if we wanted the Part to turn to the right.

                      The dimensions of a Part do not change when a Part is rotated. No matter how a
               Part is rotated, the DX of a Part is always the width, the DY of a Part is always the
               length, and the DZ of a Part is always the thickness. It's just like if you picked up a
               board from your shop and you turned it different ways, the length (DY) of that board
               would always be the length no matter what direction the board was pointed it in.

                      The X, Y, and Z-axis do not change when a Part is rotated. In other words just
               because a Part is rotated the X is still left and right, the Y is still up and down, and the
               Z is still front to back, if the Part is in reference to an Assembly.

Operands and the Order of Operations

Computation Operations

Multiplication (*) y * z = x 2 * 6 = 12

Division (/) y / z = x 12 / 6 = 2

Addition (+) y + z = x 2 + 2 = 4

Subtraction (-) y - z = x 4 - 2 = 2

Exponent (^) y^3 = x 6^2 = 36

Order of operations

Multiplication and division are always done first, then addition and subtraction. If you want to add
or subtract first and then multiply or divide you must place parenthesis around the addition or
subtraction.

Example: 24 - 6 / 3 = 22

Whereas (24 - 6) / 3 = 6

In the first example 24 - 6 / 3 = 22 the division was done first which resulted in 2 (6 / 3 = 2), then it

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
subtracted the 2 and gave us 22 (24 - 2 = 22).

In the second example (24 - 6) / 3 = 6 the operations in the parenthesis were done first which
resulted in 18 (24 - 6 = 18), then it divided the 18, which resulted in 6 (18 / 3 = 6).

As you can see the order of operations can make a big difference in the outcome of your
computation. Any operation you want done first must be placed in parenthesis. You can place
parenthesis inside of parenthesis, if need be, as many levels deep as it takes to do whatever you
are doing. Example ((((24 - 6) * (4 / 2)) + 3) * (15 - 5)) / 2 = ?

CABINET VISION starts out doing the operations in the inner most parentheses and any
multiplications and divisions not in parenthesis first, and then it just repeats until it has finished all
the operations. Every time it does an operation it is similar to removing the parenthesis around the
operations already preformed.

((((24 - 6) * (4 / 2)) + 3) * (15 - 5)) / 2 = ?

(((18 * 2) + 3) * 10) /2

((36 + 3) * 10) / 2

(39 * 10) /2

390 / 2 = 195

Types of Orientation

Normal or Front Orientation

The face of the Part is toward you. The reference point is in the left, bottom and back corner. See
"Part in Normal Orientation".

Left Orientation

The Part is rotated so that the face of the Part is facing the left and the back of the Part is facing
the inside of the Assembly. The right edge of the Part is facing the front of the Assembly. The left
edge of the Part is facing the back of the Assembly. The top of the Part is at the top. The bottom of
the Part is at the bottom. An example of a Part in left orientation would be a Left End; also all
Partitions are left oriented. The reference point would be in the right, bottom and back corner of
the Part.

Right Orientation

The Part is rotated so that the face of the Part is facing the right and the back of the Part is facing
the inside of the Assembly. The right edge of the Part is facing the back of the Assembly. The left
edge of the Part is facing toward the front of the Assembly. The top of the Part is at the top. The
bottom of the Part is at the bottom. An example of a Part in right orientation would be a Right End.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
The reference point would be in the left, bottom and front corner of the Part.

Top Orientation

The face of the Part is facing up; the back of the Part is facing the inside of the Assembly. The top
of the Part is facing the right end of the Assembly; the bottom of the Part is facing the left end of
the Assembly. The left side of the Part is facing the back of the Assembly; the right side is facing
toward the front of the Assembly. An example of a Part in top orientation would be the Top of an
Upper Cabinet or the Stretchers in a Base Cabinet. Also all Shelves in an Assembly are top
orientated. The reference point is in the left, bottom and back corner of the Part same as a Part in
normal orientation.

Bottom Orientation

The face of the Part is facing down; the back of the Part is facing the inside of the Assembly. The
left edge is facing the front of the Assembly and the right edge is facing the back of the Assembly.
The top is facing the right end of the Assembly and the bottom is facing the left end of the
Assembly. An example of a Part that is bottom oriented would be the Deck of a Base Cabinet or
the Bottom of an Upper Cabinet. The reference point is in the left, top and front corner of the Part.

                      Did you notice how the back (or unfinished side) of the Part is always facing the
               inside of the Assembly? This is because when you lay Material on a point to point
               machine, or a router, the face of the Material usually goes down with the back of the
               Material facing up. The back of the Material is where operations are typically
               performed. Therefore the back of the Material must face the inside of the Assembly
               with the face or finished side facing out.

To see the reference point

To see the reference point for different Parts right click on a Assembly and then select "Edit".
While at the Assembly Level click on one of the ortho views. Then click on a Part and its reference
point will light up. You will have to click on the same Part in two different views in order to tell
exactly where the reference point is visually.

Also if you look in the sidebar, while you have a Part high-lighted, you will see the "Left/Right",
"Up/Down", and the "In/Out" measurements as measured from the reference point of the
Assembly to the reference point of the Part you clicked on.

The AX = 0 so this Part has not been rotated on the X-axis.

The AY = -90 so this Part has been rotated on the Y-axis (clockwise) to face left.

The AZ = 0 so this Part has not been rotated on the Z-axis.

How to Differentiate Between Multiple Parts

When there is more than one part with the same name you use the "@" (at) symbol to differentiate
between them. Example say there where five boards, the first one would be BOARD or
BOARD@1, the second one would be BOARD@2 the third one would be BOARD@3, the fourth
one would be BOARD@4, Etc.

For the first part in the list you don't have to use the "@" (at) symbol. If you just type BOARD, the
program goes to the first BOARD on the list, or if you type BOARD@1 it goes to the first BOARD
on the list. It's all the same to the program, but for the other parts you must use the "@" symbol
and what number the part is in the list.

Formulas

I hope you didn't skip ahead to this section. You really need to understand everything that comes
before this or you will be lost. Writing a formula is actually fairly simple, the two basic steps are:

1. Figure out what it is you are trying to do (this is your formula) and write it down (this is the hard
    part).

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
2. Trace it through the Object Tree to get your code (this is the easy part).

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Formula Names
Notice how in the above picture, after the names of the Parts, it has letters in brackets; for the
"Finished Left End" is says LF, for the "Finished Right End" it says RF, for the "Unfinished Back" it
says UB, for the "Deck" it says DE, and for the "Top" it says TO.
These letters in brackets are the names you will be using when you write formulas. In your formula
if you wanted to refer to the "Deck", of a Base Cabinet, you would refer to it using "DE" not "Deck".
If you wanted to refer to the Top you would use "TO" not "Top".
Tracing Through The Tree
If I asked you what the height of a Cabinet was you might say 34 1/2". This is correct as far as it
goes. But to tell the computer what height the Cabinet is, is done a little differently. To tell the
computer how high the Cabinet is, you would say CAB.DY.
If you wanted to subtract the thickness of the Deck from the height of the Cabinet you would say
34 1/2 - 3/4 = 33 3/4". To tell the computer the height of the Cabinet minus the thickness of the
deck, we would say CAB.DY - CAB.CASE.DE.DZ. To come up with this information you need to
trace it through the Object Tree. See the following picture. Let's take the height of the Cabinet
minus the thickness of the Deck and trace it through the tree. First we want the height of the
Cabinet.
Open the Object Tree (see Object Tree "Assembly Level") and click on the Cabinet to highlight it. Then
look down at the lower pane and the parameter for the height of the Cabinet is "DY". So the height
of the Cabinet is CAB.DY. The very top level of the Object Tree (when you are dealing with an
Assembly) is called CAB. It doesn't matter what the name of the Assembly is, for formulas it is
called CAB.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Next get the thickness of the Deck. Open the Object Tree up even more until you find the Deck.
Starting at the top (CAB) and working your way down, the thickness of the Deck is
CAB.CASE.DE.DZ.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Where are we coming up with those periods? Well every time the tree branches we add a
"period". Notice that in the case of the Deck it starts at the top (CAB) and then it branches at Case
so you add a period between the word CAB and the word Case. Next it branches at the Deck so
you add a period between Case and DE and you have CAB.CASE.DE. From the Deck you move
to the parameters in the bottom pane. Any time you move from the top pane to the bottom pane
you add a period so you must place a period between DE and the parameter DZ (DZ = thickness
which is what you are looking for) and you have CAB.CASE.DE.DZ, which is the thickness of the
Deck. So the height of the Cabinet minus the thickness of the deck is equal to CAB.DY-
CAB.CASE.DE.DZ.
Say you wanted to know the width of the Adjustable Shelf minus the thickness of the Adjustable
Shelf Strip. First you would open up the Object Tree until you found the Adjustable Shelf. See the
following picture. If you trace the first part, the width of the Adjustable Shelf through the tree you
come up with CAB.INTERIOR.AS.DX. If you trace the second part through the tree you come up
with CAB.INTERIOR.AS.SS.DZ. Putting these two together you come up with
CAB.INTERIOR.AS.DX - CAB.INTERIOR.AS.SS.DZ.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
So how does CAB.INTERIOR.AS.DX - CAB.INTERIOR.AS.SS.DZ work? Well, it is like a road
map for CABINET VISION. The first part CAB.INTERIOR.AS.DX leads CABINET VISION to the
DX parameter of the "AS" (Adjustable Shelf), which in this case has a value of 22 23/32 inches.
The second part CAB.INTERIOR.AS.SS.DZ leads CABINET VISION to the DZ parameter of the
"SS" (Adjustable Shelf Strip), which has a value of 3/4 inches. The whole thing basically tells
CABINET VISION 22 23/32 - 3/4 = 21 31/32.
First Exercise
Writing Formulas
If you read the beginning of this document and you work your way through the following
"Exercises". You will be well on your way to understanding how to add intelligence to parts you
add to an object. Be that object a cabinet or something you are creating from scratch like a
corbel, a wood top, a can goods rack, a fireplace mantel, a store fixture of some kind, or whatever.
Understanding formulas will also help you with any "User Created Standards" (UCS) you may
wish to write. "User Created Standards" can do a lot, but they can do a lot more when you know a
little about writing formulas. So it is going to be well worth your time to read the beginning of this
document and to work your way through all the exercises presented.
First Exercise
So lets add a part to a cabinet and give it intelligence by writing formulas for its placement and
sizing. We will not need to write a formula for the rotation, as once we get the part rotated into
place, it will not need to rotate again. What we are going to do is start a Frameless job and place
a base cabinet. Once the base cabinet is placed we will turn it into a sink cabinet. The sink
cabinet will have a false front and a butt pair of doors. We will then add a part behind the false
front so we can screw through it to hold the false front in place. And then we will give it intelligence
by writing formulas for it placement and sizing.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Very Important! Preliminary Setup for the Exercises
Before we start it is very important that you setup a Frameless construction method, for base
cabinets, that has what is called a "Standard End". When you run the Part Wizard for the finished
ends select "Standard End" as the end type. See picture below.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Under the "Top" area set your construction to use "Top Stretchers", and set them to butt into the
sides of the cabinet. The "Bottom" must also be set to butt into the sides of the cabinet. Set your
"Toe Kick Height" to 4 1/4" high.
Also it is important that you setup a cabinet part "Material Schedule" that is using 3/4" material for
the finished and unfinished ends, the Deck, the Top Stretchers, and 3/4" material for the part
called "Board". The part called "Board" can be found under "Face" and then "Face Frame". This
way we will all be on the same page and you will be able to follow along with the sample code we
will be writing.

2. On the "Material" tab make sure that you select the cabinet part material schedule that you

    setup earlier.

4. Click on the cabinet and in the sidebar change the "Width" to 36 inches. Change the "Height" to

    34-1/2 inches, Change the "Depth" to 24 inches (don't skip any steps).
5. Right click on the cabinet and select "Edit".

Answer yes when it asks you if you want to continue.

approximately where the crack between the false front and the doors would be. You should

now have a Cabinet with a drawer above a door.

10. Click on the drawer opening and then select "False Front" from the sidebar.

11. Click on the door opening and then select "Pair Door" from the sidebar.

Cabinet. It should have top stretchers, a false front, no shelves, and a pair of doors.

                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.

      "Change". Changing the material here instead of in your material schedule will "Lock" the
      material to always use the material you select here. If you later changed the Material Schedule
      expecting the material for this board to change with the Material Schedule it would not

      you entered and it wouldn't change when you changed your Material Schedule. You will notice
      something called "Relate to Cabinet Part" you will not check this. This is used to give a part
      intelligence without you having to write formulas. For now we will do it the old fashioned way.
       Which is actually better because you will need to know how to do this for yourself,
      anyway. And because when you let the computer do it for you it doesn't always write the most
      flexible formula. When done entering the length and width click on "Next".

  cabinet it is add to. This is to get the part out of the way so you can find it.

  The first thing we are going to do is to manually rotate this part so it is going in the correct

                                                                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
  direction. We want to it to lay to the right with the length going left and right. Then we will
  manually place it where it needs to go in the cabinet. We will then begin to write formulas for it. In

The part is now rotated and positioned correctly and we are ready to give the part intelligence.
First Exercise Formula for the X (Left/Right)

Look at your cabinet in 3D. Look at it from a Face  ortho view and click on the BOARD.

Notice where the reference point is located. Look at it from a side view, click on the BOARD.

Notice where the reference point is located. When writing code for the position of a part it is

important to know where the reference point is.

© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
We will need a formula for the X (Left/Right) because if the thickness of the end changes this part
will need to move left or right.
As far as a formula for the X position of the BOARD, there are several that could work. We could
say that the X of the Board was equal to the thickness of the left end. However, when writing
formulas it is best to avoid using the ends in your code if at all possible. The reason for this is
that there are 10 different end "Types". We would have to write 10 formulas, one for each end
type. See the following picture.

Example if we said the X position of the Board was equal to the thickness of the left unfinished
end and there was no left unfinished end, our code would not work. The part could end up
positioned wrong or not appearing in the cabinet at all. So we need to think up a different formula.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
                      When writing formulas the easiest thing to do is just to find something in the
               cabinet that already has the value you need and that will change in the way you want
               the parameter you are working on to change.

If you look at the cabinet in 3D you can see that the Deck, the Top Stretchers, and the Nailers are
all butted into the left side of the cabinet the same as this BOARD. If the thickness of the end
changes the Deck, the Top Stretchers, and the Nailers will all move in relation to the thickness of
the end. So we could use the X position of any of these parts as the X position of our board.

                      When choosing what you want to use as the reference for adding intelligence, be
               sure that you do not choose something that may change later on. As an example, if
               you relate a part to the size of a mid stile, and later on, you delete the mid stile from
               the cabinet, the formula you wrote will be invalid.

We will use the X position of the Deck as the X position of our Board. So our formula will be the X
of the Board = the X of the Deck. Now that we know what our formula is, we only have to trace it
through the Object Tree. So we can put it in a language the computer can understand.

1. Open the Object Tree by clicking on one of the ortho  views, then click on

"Object Tree". We then open the tree up until we find the Deck (notice the BOARD we added

is showing right under the cabinet), we highlight the deck and then we click on the parameter

we want, the X. We then trace it (the X of the Deck) through the tree starting at the top and

working our way down to the X, and the code we come up with is "CAB.CASE.DE.X". We write

this down so we don't forget it, or highlight the path in the Object Tree path bar (highlighted in

the illustration below) to the Windows Clipboard.

2. Now we go to the part we want to write the formula for. So while still in the Object Tree click on
    the BOARD. Then click on the X, this is the parameter we wish to write the formula for.

3. With the X highlighted, click on the "Edit parameter" button in the Object Tree. This will open
    the "Parameter Edit" screen. Notice the "Name" of the parameter is "X" and notice that it is set
    to a "Value" of 3/4".

4. Select Equation, the "Add", "Delete", and "Test" buttons will all be highlighted. And the "IF" line
    and the "THEN" line will also be highlighted.

The IF Line

             © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
The "If" line, and the "THEN" line, are the lines you will be writing your formula, or code on. The
"IF" line is used to set a "condition" that must be true before your code will execute. For
example you could say Cab.Name = 'Sink' this means that the name of the cabinet must be
"Sink" or the program will not execute the code on the THEN line. We are not going to go into it
that deep at this time, so we will not be changing anything on the IF line. You will notice that the
IF line has a 1 on it, 1 means true, so anything we write on the THEN line will execute.

The THEN Line

The "THEN" line is where we write what we want the program to do, if the condition on the IF line
is true. This is where we will write the code that we wrote down earlier.

5. Click on the "THEN" line and remove the "0". Then type in the code we wrote down earlier
    "CAB.CASE.DE.X", do not type in the quotation marks.

Note: It makes no difference to the computer if you type your code all in upper case letters, or all
in lower case letters, or in some "Combination" of the two.

Testing your Formula

After typing in the code you always want to "Test" your code to make sure it is working.

6. Click on the "Test" Button. In the "Test Result" area it should say "Condition returned: True.
     Equation returned: 3/4." Or whatever value you were expecting.

7. Click on "OK". This will return you to the Object Tree and you will see the result of your
    equation.

8. Look at your cabinet in 3D does it look OK? If not you typed something wrong. See
    "Troubleshooting Error Messages".

Formula for the Y (Up/Down)

Look at your cabinet in 3D. Look at it from a front ortho view and click on the BOARD. Notice
where the reference point is located. Look at it from a side view. Notice where the reference point
is located. When writing code for the position of a part it is important to know where the reference
point is.

There are several formulas that will work for the Y position of this BOARD. You will learn as time
goes by that there is always more than one way to do things in Solid. We could say the Y is
equal to the height of the cabinet minus the thickness of the top stretcher. Or we could say
the Y is equal to the height of the cabinet minus 3/4". It would be better to use the first
formula because if the thickness of the top stretcher changed the first formula would take this into

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
consideration whereas the second formula would not. We could say the Y of the BOARD is equal
to the Y of the top stretcher. If you click on the top stretcher you will note that it and the BOARD
have the same up and down position. This is a good formula so we will use it. The Y of the
BOARD = the Y of the Top Stretcher. So now that we have our formula. We need to trace it
through the object tree.

1. Click on one of the ortho  views.

2. Click on "Object Tree".

3. Open the Object Tree until you find the Top Stretcher, click on it and then click on the Y
    parameter on the right. If we trace this through the tree it is CAB.CASE.TS.Y we write this
    code down so we don't forget it.

4. Click on the BOARD then click on the Y parameter.

5. Click on "Edit". Your screen should now look like the follow screen.

6. Select Equation and then on the THEN line type the code we wrote down earlier.
    CAB.CASE.TS.Y.

7. Click on the test button and it should say "Condition returned: True. Equation returned: 33 3/4
    or whatever value you were expecting. Click on OK.

Look at your cabinet in 3D does it look OK? If not you typed something wrong. See "Troubleshooting
Error Messages".

First Exercise Formula for the Z (Front/Back)

Look at your cabinet in 3D. Look at it from the End view. Notice where the reference point is
located. When writing code for the position of a part it is important to know where the reference
point is.

There are several formulas that will work for the Z position of this BOARD. We could say the
depth of the cabinet minus 3/4". Or we could say the depth of the cabinet minus the
thickness of the BOARD (this is better because if the BOARD changes thickness this one would
take that into consideration, whereas the first one wouldn't). If your deck is 24" wide we could say
the width of the deck minus the thickness of the BOARD. Or we could say the width of the
deck minus ¾". We will use the depth of the cabinet minus the thickness of the BOARD as
our formula. So now that we have our formula. We need to trace it through the object tree and
convert it to code.

1. Click on one of the ortho  views.
2. Click on "Object Tree".

                              © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
3. Click on the cabinet name and then click on the depth of the cabinet (DZ). Trace it through the
    tree and it is Cab.Dz write this down this is the first part of our code.

4. Click on the BOARD and then click on the thickness (DZ). Trace it through the tree and it is
    Cab.Board.Dz this is the second part or our code write it down.

5. Combine the two together and we get Cab.Dz - Cab.Board.Dz write it down.

6. We should already be on the BOARD so all we have to do is click on the Z and then click on
    "Edit".

    or whatever value you were expecting. Click on OK.

The width of the BOARD is 4" this is never going to change so we don't need to write a formula for

Formula for the DY (Length)

Look at your cabinet in 3D. Look at it from a front ortho view and click on the BOARD. Notice
where the reference point is located. When writing code that sizes a part it is important to know
where the reference point is. Because when the part changes size it could also change position, if
your not careful how you orient the part.

There are several formulas that will work for the DY of the BOARD. We could say the width of
the cabinet minus the thickness of the two ends. But we already know to stay away from the
ends if we can. We could say the width of the cabinet minus 1 1/2", but if the thickness of the
ends changed this code wouldn't work very well. Like I said earlier the easiest thing to do is find
something in the cabinet that all ready has the value you need and that will change in the way you
want the parameter you are working on to change.

If you look at the cabinet in 3D you can see that the Deck, the Top Stretchers, and the Nailers are
all butted between the sides of the cabinet, the same as this BOARD. If the thickness of ether end
changes the Deck, the Top Stretchers, and the Nailers will all change size in relation to the
thickness of the ends. Also, if the cabinet is stretched so that it is wider, these parts will grow. So
we could use the DY of any of these parts as the DY of our board. We will use the DY of the
deck for the DY of our BOARD. So our formula is: the length of the deck. So now that we have
our formula. We need to trace it through the object tree to get our code.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
1. Click on one of the ortho                views.

2. Click on "Object Tree".

3. Open the object tree until you can see the Deck.

4. Click on the DY parameter. Trace it through the tree and it is Cab.Case.De.Dy write this down,
    this is the code we need.

5. Click on the BOARD and then click on the length (the DY) then click on "Edit".

6. Change from a "Value" to an "Equation".

7. On the THEN line type in the code we came up with Cab.Case.De.Dy.

8. Click on the "Test" button and it should say "Condition returned: True. Equation returned: 34
    1/2 or whatever value you were expecting. Click on OK.

9. Look at your cabinet in 3D does it look OK? If not you typed something wrong. See
    "Troubleshooting Error Messages".

Try changing the size of the cabinet the width, the height and the depth. The BOARD we added
should move and size correctly. When done put it back to the original size. You might want to
save the cabinet back into your library so you can do the second example exercise later.

Steps to Writing a Formula

Steps to writing a Formula

By now you should see a pattern developing.

1. Add a part. Size the part correctly and place the part correctly.

2. Select a part to work on. You might have more than one. If you have more than one part that
    needs intelligence, pick one part to work on.

3. What is it you are trying to do to this part? Are you trying to place it left and right (X) or up and
    down (Y) or in and out (Z) or are you sizing it for width (DX) or length (DY)? Pick one
    parameter to work on at a time.

4. Write your formula out in English first! Make sure you write it down so you won't get confused
    later. Example formula, the height of the cabinet minus the height of the toe kick.

5. Trace it through the Object Tree, and write it down! If your formula has more than one part
    trace each part of the formula separately.

6. The first level of the Object Tree is always "CAB" no matter what the name of the object is.

                              © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 7. Every time the tree branches add a period.

 8. When you step through each level of the tree add a period.

 9. Go back to the Part you are working on. After you have traced it through the tree and written
      the code down, click back on the Part you want to work on.

10. Select the Parameter you want to work on.

11. Select "Edit".

12. Change from a "Value" to an "Equation".

13. Write your code on the "THEN" line.

14. Always "Test" your code (If possible, some code may rely on other code you haven't finished
      writing yet.).

15. Always go back and look at your assembly in 3D (at the Assembly Level) and see if it still looks
      OK.

  Troubleshooting Error Messages

  There are three reasons for 95% of the errors returned when writing a formula:

 1. A part name (or code) has been entered incorrectly or misspelled. Example; Cab.Casse.De.X
      notice that Case is misspelled.

 2. The periods within your "then" statement have been left out, or a comma was entered.

 3. The path to the part is not correct. For instance looking at the Object Tree, you'll see that the
      Adjustable Shelf (code AS) (if this cabinet had one), is under the "Interior", not the "Case".

     a. IF your statement used "cab.case.as.dx", (to refer to the adjustable shelf width), an error
          would be returned. The correct statement would be "cab.interior.as.dx".

  The path is evident by looking at the Object Tree, and looking "up" to the parent of the part in
  question, or by looking "down" from the cabinet to the part and parameter in question. It is
  structured much like a "branching" tree.

  So lets add another part to the cabinet. This time we will add a BOARD but it will be going up and
  down and it will fit between the BOARD we have already placed and the deck. Also it will be
  centered in the cabinet left to right. See following picture. In order to see what we are doing we
  will delete the false front and the pair of butt doors.

1. Click on the "Section" button and then make sure the "Section Face" button is selected.

    first BOARD we added.

4. Click on "Next". This will bring you to the "Size" tab.

5. If you where to measure the distance from the bottom of the BOARD to the deck it would be 24
    3/4" (proved you did the preliminary setup you where supposed to do). So set the length to 24

6. On the "Orientation" tab select "Front" orientation. It is easier for most people to add parts in
    "Front" orientation and then later rotate them into position at an ortho view. Click on "Next".

7. You should now be at the "Finish" tab. For this demonstration the finish doesn't matter. Click
    on the "Finish" button.

You will note that the part came in with a "Left/Right" of -18". Whenever a part is manually added
to a cabinet it will always come in with a "Left/Right" equal to one half the width of whatever
cabinet it is added to. This is to get the part out of the way so you can find it.

8. The part is all ready going in the correct direction. But it needs to be centered in the cabinet,
    one half of the width of the cabinet (the cabinet should be 36") is 18" but the reference point
    for the BOARD is on the left side, so we can't just say the "Left/Right is 18, because the
    BOARD would be off center. So we must subtract one half the width of the part from the

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
      18". 18 - 2 = 16 so we enter 16 into the "Left/Right" and press enter.

 9. It now needs to move up to the top of the deck. If you set your "Toe Kick" height to 4 1/4" and
      your bottom material to 3/4" thick, this adds up to 5", type 5" into the "Up/Down" area and press
      enter.

10. It now needs to move to the front of the cabinet (24 - .75 = 23.25), so we enter 23 1/4" were it
      says "In/Out" and press enter.

  The part is now rotated and positioned correctly and we are ready to give the part intelligence.

  Formula for the X (Left/Right)

  Look at your cabinet in 3D. Look at it from a front ortho view and click on the second BOARD.
  Notice where the reference point is located. Look at it from a top view and from a side view, click
  on the BOARD. Notice where the reference point is located. When writing code for the position of
  a part it is important to know where the reference point is.

  We will need a formula for the X because the BOARD is centered in the cabinet. If the width of
  the cabinet were ever to change the BOARD would need to move so that it stayed centered. Also
  what if the width of the board were to change? This would also throw off the centering.

  See if you can come up with the formula for centering the BOARD yourself. Hint; you already
  know what the formula is because you centered the board in the cabinet to start off with.

  Before we continue you will need to know a little about "operands" and the "order" of mathematical
  operations.

  Second Exercise for the X Part 2

  See if you can come up with the formula for centering the BOARD yourself. You already know it
  because you used it to center the BOARD in the cabinet in the first place.

  The BOARD needs to be centered in the cabinet, so we need to know what the center of the
  cabinet is. The center of the cabinet is one half of the width of the cabinet. But first we need to
  know the width of the cabinet so we can divide it in half. So we trace the width of the cabinet
  through the tree and it is "Cab.Dx". One half of the cabinet width would be "Cab.Dx/2". So the
  first part of our formula is "Cab.Dx/2". We would write it down so we wouldn't get confused later.

  The reference point for the second BOARD is on the left side, so we can't just say the X is half the
  width of the cabinet, because the second BOARD would be off center. We must subtract one half
  the width of the second BOARD from the center of the cabinet. But first we need to know what
  the width of the second BOARD is so we can divide it in half. If you trace it through the tree you
  will notice that there are two Boards. See the following picture.

                                                                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
We want the width of the second BOARD, but how do we tell the program that we want the width
of the second BOARD not the first BOARD seeing as they both have the same name?

Second Exercise for the X Part 3

Our formula is one half the width of the cabinet minus one half the width of the BOARD, or
width of cabinet /2 - width of second BOARD /2.

We could also say width of cabinet minus width of second BOARD then the whole thing
divided by two.

When you trace it through the tree:

Width of cabinet / 2 - width of second BOARD / 2 it equals Cab.Dx/2 - Cab.BOARD@2.DX/2

Width of cabinet minus width of second BOARD then the whole thing divided by two would
equal (Cab.Dx - Cab.BOARD@2.Dx) / 2 same thing really.

We'll use the first one Cab.Dx/2 - Cab.BOARD@2.DX/2 as our code.

1. Go to the Object Tree from the Assembly Level (click on one of the ortho
    views and then click on "Object Tree").

2. Click on the second board (the bottom one). Click on the X parameter. Click on "Edit".

3. Change it from a "Value" to an "Equation".

4. On the "THEN" line type the code. Cab.Dx/2 - Cab.BOARD@2.DX/2.

5. Click on the test button and it should say "Condition returned: True. Equation returned: 16 or
    whatever value you were expecting. Click on OK.

Look at your cabinet in 3D does it look OK? If not you will have to trouble shoot what you just did.

Formula for the Y (Up/Down)

Look at your cabinet from a Face  ortho view and click on the second BOARD. Notice

where the reference point is located. Click on some of the other parts in the cabinet (especially

the deck). Notice where the reference point is located. When writing code for the position of a

part it is important to know where the reference point for that part is in relation to the reference

points for the other parts.

Looking at the cabinet from a front ortho view there are several formulas that will work. We could
say the Y is equal to the width of the front toe (the front toe is laying down so its "Width" is
running up and down, not left and right) plus the thickness of the deck. So the formula could be
width of front toe plus thickness of deck. Or, if you click on the deck and then you click on the
second BOARD you will notice that they have the same Y position. So we could say the Y of the

                                  © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
board is equal to the Y of the deck. We will use the second formula the Y of the deck.
1. Go to the Object Tree and open it up until you see the deck.
2. Click on the Deck and then click on the Y parameter. Trace it through the tree and write it

    down, it should be "Cab.Case.De.y".
3. Click on the second BOARD. Then click on the Y parameter.
4. Click on "Edit".
5. Change from a "Value" to an "Equation".
6. On the THEN line type in the code you traced through the tree.
7. Click on the "Test" button and it should say "Condition returned: True. Equation returned: 5 or

    whatever value you were expecting. Click on OK.
Look at your cabinet in 3D does it look OK? If not you will have to trouble shoot what you just did.

Formula for the Z (Front/Back)

Look at your cabinet from an End  ortho view and click on the second BOARD. Notice

where the reference point is located. Click on some of the other parts in the cabinet (especially

the first board). Notice where the reference point is located.

There are several formulas that will work. We could say the Z of Board@2 is equal to the Z of the
deck minus the thickness of board@2. Click on the Deck and notice where the Z is. We could
say it is equal to the depth of the cabinet minus the thickness of board@2. We could say it is
equal to the Z position of the front stretcher plus the width of the front stretcher minus the
thickness of board@2. We could say the Z of board@2 is equal to the Z of board@1. I think
well use this last one; the Z of board@2 is equal to the Z of board@1. When we trace the Z of
board@1 through the tree it is Cab.Board@1.Z or just Cab.Board.Z we don't have to put in the
"@" symbol for the first part in a list of similarly named parts.

1. Go to the Object Tree and click on the first BOARD. Then click on the Z parameter. When we
    trace the Z of board@1 through the tree it is Cab.Board@1.Z or just Cab.Board.Z we don't
    have to put in the "@" symbol for the first part in a list if we don't want to.

2. Click on the second BOARD. Then click on the Z parameter.

3. Click on "Edit" and change from a "Value" to an "Equation".

4. On the THEN line type the code you traced through the tree.

5. Click the "Test" button and it should say "Condition returned: True. Equation returned: 23 1/4
    or whatever value you were expecting. Click on OK.

Formula for the DY (Length)

Look at your cabinet in 3D. Look at it from a Face       ortho view and click on the BOARD.

Notice where the reference point is located. Click on several of the other parts and notice where

their reference points are located.

There are several formulas that will work. We could say the DY of board@2 is equal to the
height of the cabinet (DY) minus the width (DX) of the front toe minus the thickness (DZ) of
the deck minus the thickness (DZ) of the top stretcher minus the width (DX) of board@1.
Or we could say the DY of board@2 was equal to the height (DY) of the "Case" minus the
thickness (DZ) of the deck minus the thickness (DZ) of the top stretcher minus the width
(DX) of board@1.

Note: If you go into your Object Tree and open it until you see the "Case" and if you click on the
"Case" you will see that the DY of the case is the DY of the cabinet minus the toe kick height (DX
of the front toe, as the toe is laying on its side so the width (DX) is up and down). So using the DY
of the "Case" could save us a little on our formula.

Or we could say the DY of board@2 is equal to the Y of board@1 minus the width of board@1
minus the Y of the deck. There are more but we'll use this one.

Y (up and down) of board@1 = 33.75"

Width (DX) of Board@1 = 4"

Y (up and down) of Deck = 5"

33.75" - 4" = 29.75"

29.75" - 5" = 24.75" the length of board@2

1. Open up your Object Tree until you can see the deck.

2. Click on the deck and then click on the Y trace it through the tree. Write it down. Answer
    Cab.Case.De.Y.

3. Click on BOARD@1 and then click on the Y. Trace it through the tree. Write it down. Answer
    Cab.Board@1.Y.

4. You should be on BOARD@1. Click on the width of BOARD@1 Trace it through the tree and

                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
    write it down. Answer Cab.Board@1.Dx.

5. Combine the code together the Y of board#1 minus the width of board#1 minus the Y of
    the deck. Answer Cab.Board@1.Y - Cab.Board@1.dx - Cab.Case.De.Y.

6. Click on BOARD@2 then click on the DY.

7. Click on "Edit" and then change from a "Value" to an "Equation".

8. Write your code on the THEN line.

9. Click the "Test" button and it should say "Condition returned: True. Equation returned: 24 3/4
    or whatever value you were expecting. Click on OK.

Look at your cabinet in 3D does it look OK?

Try changing the size of the cabinet the width, the height and the depth. The BOARD we added
should move and size correctly. You might want to save the cabinet back into your library so you
can do the third example exercise later. Don't forget to size the cabinet back to its original size.

Third Exercise

So lets add another part to the cabinet and make it even more interesting. This time we will add a
BOARD but it will be going left and right placed to fit between the BOARD@2 we have already
placed and the right side of the cabinet. It will be centered in the cabinet opening up and down
between BOARD@1 and the deck. See following picture.

1. Click on the "Face"  ortho view tab, and then click on the "New Part" button. When the

"New Part" screen comes up, under the "Part Type" area select "Board".

                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
2. Click on "Next". This will bring you to the "Size" tab.

3. If you where to measure the distance from the right side of BOARD@2 and the side of the
    cabinet it would be 15 1/4. So set the length to 15 1/4", set the "Width" to 4". Leave the
    thickness alone. Click on "Next".

4. On the "Orientation" tab select "Front" orientation. Click on "Next".

5. You should now be at the "Finish" tab. For this demonstration the finish doesn't matter. Click
    on the "Finish" button.

The first thing we are going to do is to manually rotate this part so it is going in the correct
direction. We want to it to tip to the right with the length going left and right. Then we will
manually place it where it needs to go in the cabinet. We will then begin to write formulas for it. If
you are not at a front ortho view, click on it now. To rotate the part so that it is laying on its right
side.

6. Click on the part to highlight it. On the left side of your screen where it says, "Rotate part by..."
    we will need to enter a negative (-) 90 degrees. The part will be hinging on the Z-axis to rotate
    down to the right. We are already facing the reference point, so to rotate the part clockwise it
    needs to be a negative amount. See "Positive (+) and Negative (-) Rotation ". Enter -90 and press
    enter.

7. We now need to place the part "Left/Right" if your cabinet is still 36" wide, and you have done
    everything you were supposed to up till now, the "Left/Right" would be 20". Half the width of
    the cabinet (18") plus half the width of BOARD#2 (2"). 18 + 2 = 20.

8. We now need to place the part "Up/Down" if your cabinet is still 34 1/2" and you have done
    everything you were supposed to up till now the "Up/Down" will be 19 3/8". The up and down
    (Y) of BOARD#2 plus half the length (DY) of BOARD#2 plus half the width (DX) of
    BOARD#3.

9. It now needs to move to the front of the cabinet (24 - .75 = 23.25), so we enter 23 1/4" were it
    says "In/Out" and press enter.

The part is now rotated and positioned correctly and we are ready to give the part intelligence.

 6. Go back to the part you are working on (board@4 - After you have traced it through the tree
      and written your code down).

 7. Select the parameter you want to work on. You are working on the DY.
 8. Select "Edit".

  Fifth Exercise
  Now for something different, we will be creating a Corbel or Counter Top Support from a Base
  Object. See picture below. A "Base Object" is a base cabinet that has been set to a default
  cabinet and then had all the parts deleted. It is used to create your own objects from scratch.
  Very Important! Preliminary Setup for the Fifth Exercises
  Before starting this exercise it is important to setup a material schedule that is using a board stock
  material for the part called board.

                                                                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Fifth Exercise Adding the First Part

1. Start a new Job. On the Job Properties screen, on the "Materials" tab, select a Material
    Schedule that is using a board stock Material for the part called "Board".

2. Draw a wall, 48 inches long is good enough.
3. Place the "Empty Base Object" on the wall. You can find the "Empty Base Object" in the

    Custom Cabinet catalog under Bases. If you don't have the "Empty Base Object":
    a. Place a standard base cabinet on the Wall.
    b. Right click on it and select "Edit".
    c. Click on the "Section Face" tab and then click on "Modifications" and "Default Assembly",

        answer "Yes" when you get the warning.
    d. Click on "Parts" and then "Delete Parts", check "All Parts" and click on "OK".
    e. Click on the "Return" option until it will not go any more.
4. Click on the Empty Base Object and size it to 2.5 inches wide, 12 inches high, and 12 inches
    deep.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
5. Right click on the Empty Base Object and select "Edit".

Look at the base object from the different ortho views. You will see that you don't have any parts.
 All your screen shows is an empty cabinet 2.5"W, 12"H, and 12"D.

6. Click on a Face      ortho view.

7. Click on "New Part", we will add the top piece first.

8. In the "Part Type" area select "Board" as the part type then click "Next". Note Under the
    "Material" area it should have a material listed that is 3/4" thick. If not DO NOT click on
    "Change". Changing the material here instead of in your material schedule will "Lock" the
    material to always use the material you select here. If you later changed the material schedule
    expecting the material for this board to change with the material schedule it would not
    change. Stop now, exit the job, go to your material catalog, click on "Schedule" at the top of
    the screen, then select "Cabinet Parts". When the "Setup Material Schedule" screen comes
    up, select one of your material schedules to work on. Click on the Plus (+) in front of "Face" to
    open it then click on the plus (+) in front of "Face Frame". Select a material for "Board" that is
    3/4" thick. Then start over from step #1 or you could reopen this job and use the "Update
    Materials" option. When you get to the "Job Properties" screen be sure to go to the "Materials"
    tab and select the material schedule that you worked on.

9. In the "Size" window set the size of this part to 12"L and 2.5"W, leave the thickness alone. This
    part is the top piece and its length will be what ever the depth of the cabinet is in this case 12".
     The width of this part is the same as the width of the cabinet in this case 2.5". Click on "Next".

10. In the "Orientation" window leave the orientation set to "Front". Click on "Next".

11. In the "Finish" window set the finish to "Exterior" for the front, back, and edges. Click on the
      "Finish" button.

You will now be at a front ortho view and on the left side of your screen the "Left/Right" will be
"-1.25 inches".

12. Set the "Left/Right" to 0 inches and press enter. This will move the part so that it is inside of
      the empty cabinet.

This part is going to be the top piece of our corbel so we are going to have to lay it face down and
then raise it up to the top of the empty cabinet. If you click on this part from different ortho views
you can see that the reference point is in the left, bottom, and back corner. In order to lay this
piece face down it is the X-axis that is going to act like a hinge. In order to face the reference
point we will need to view the part from a "Right" ortho view.

13. Click on the "End"  ortho view tab. We want to lay this part face down and to do that we

will need to rotate it "counter clockwise". To rotate it counter clockwise we will need to enter a

positive amount. See "Positive (+) and Negative (-) Rotation". Click on the part and enter +90 in the

"Rotation" area, you must press enter after entering the +90.

                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
  As you can see the reference point is now on top of the part. And the part is below the empty
  cabinet. In order to raise the part to the top of the empty cabinet we will need to enter 12" in the
  "Up/Down" area.

14. Enter 12 in the "Up/Down" area and press enter.

  This part is now rotated and positioned correctly so we will now add the back piece.

  Fifth Exercise Adding the Second Part

1. Click on a "Face"  ortho view and then click on "New Part".

2. In the "Part Type" area select "Board" as the new part, click on "Next".

Fifth Exercise Adding the Third Part

1. Click on a Face    ortho view.

2. Click on "New Part". We will be adding the center-piece. In the "Part Type" area select
    "Board" as the part type then click "Next".

3. In the "Size" window set the size to be 10.75"L by 10.75"W. This is the center-piece of our
    corbel and it will be running up and down with its "Face" facing left. Its length will be the height
    of the cabinet minus the thickness of board@1 minus .5" just to make it look better (12 - .75 =
    11.25) (11.25 - .5 = 10.75). Its width will be the depth of the cabinet minus the thickness of
    board@2 minus .5" just to make it look better (12 - .75 = 11.25) (11.25 - .5 = 10.75). Click on
    "Next".

4. In the "Orientation" window leave the orientation set to "Front". Click on "Next".

                      © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
5. In the "Finish" window set the finish to "Exterior" for the front, back, and edges. Click on the
    "Finish" button.

You will now be at a Face  ortho view and on the left side of your screen the "Left/Right" will

be "-1.25". Before we position the part we will rotate it. Looking at the corbel from different ortho

views                   and also looking at it from the 3D view we can see that this part needs to

turn so that the "Face" of the part is facing left. In order to turn the part to face left it is the Y-axis

that will be acting like a hinge. In order to face the reference point we will have to look at this last

piece from a "Plan"        ortho view.

6. Click on the "Plan"     ortho view tab.

7. Click on the part. In the "Rotation" area we will need to enter a "-90" for the part to rotate
    clockwise. Enter -90 and press enter.

Look at where the reference point for this part is located. This part needs to be centered in the
cabinet left and right, one half of the width of the cabinet (the cabinet should be 2.5") is 1.25"
but the reference point for the BOARD is on the right side, so we can't just say the "Left/Right" is
1.25", because the BOARD would be off center. So we must add one half the thickness of the
part to the 1.25". 1.25 + .375 = 1.625.

8. So we enter 1.625 into the "Left/Right" and press enter.

Look at this part; notice where the reference point is located as you can see the board needs to
moved forward by the thickness of board@2.

9. Type .75 into the "In/Out" area and press enter.

10. The part needs to move up .5" type .5 in the "Up/Down" area and press enter.

All three parts are now rotated and positioned correctly, and we are ready to give them
intelligence. So that if we change the width, height, or depth of the cabinet the parts will grow, and
shrink, and move accordingly.

Fifth Exercise Notes on Formulas

In the section that follows, I want you to think about whether or not we need a formula for the
parameter in question. Do we? Think about it a little. What should happen to the parts if we
change the width, height or depth of the corbel? If you need help you can click on "Answer".

I want you to try and come up with the formula yourself. Think about how the parts are related to
the overall size of the corbel, and the other parts in the corbel. Click on each piece and notice
where the reference point is and how it relates to the reference point of the corbel (left, bottom,
and back corner). If you need help you can click on "Formula".

Once you have written down your formula, trace it through the tree to get the code and write the

                           © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
code down. If you need help you can click on "Code".
I have purposely left out the step-by-step instructions for giving the parts intelligence; if you did the
four exercises up till now you should know the steps. If you need help refer to the section "Steps to
writing a Formula" in the first exercise.
There is more than one way to skin a cat, so you may come up with a different formula and code
than the samples shown here. If you do, try your code and see what happens. If it works, great!
Then compare it to what is shown here and see which one you like best.

What We Learned
· You should have noticed that any time the X, Y, or Z is equal to 0" you don't have to write a

   formula for the placement parameter.
· You should have noticed that we didn't write any formulas for the thickness of the parts, the

   thickness of the parts comes from the material the part is made from.
· You should have noticed that you didn't write any formulas for the AX, AY, or AZ. You almost

   never have to write a formula for the rotation because once a part is rotated into place it almost
   never changes rotation.
· You should have noticed that if you size and place the part correctly to start with, you are using
   the formulas you need to size and place the part.
Shaping the Corbel
Now that you have created the corbel and given the parts intelligence you may wish to shape
board@3 so it looks more like a corbel. When you shape anything in Solid and then later change
the size of the object that was shaped, the shape will distort. In order to control the shape and not
have it distort you must "constrain" certain entities which make up the shape. The following
exercises are designed to teach you how to shape a part and constrain it so that the shape
doesn't distort.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
For the first exercise in shaping a part we will take the above corbel and shape it to look like the
following corbel.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
If you are not already at the Assembly Level, right click on your corbel and select "Edit".

1. Click on the End  ortho view tab.

2. Right click on Board@3 and select "Edit Shape".

                      You would not use the "Edit Shape" button in the sidebar, because you would be
               shaping the entire object or assembly. We have not given the parts any intelligence for
               changing shape when the assembly changes shape, so shaping the entire assembly
               would have no effect on any of the parts.

3. The first thing you want to do is add some reference lines to use to create the clip. We want the
    clip to start and end at 2 inches. So, use the Modify | Offset option to offset the top and back
    lines in 2 inches.

4. Now that you have your reference lines in place make sure that "Snap to Points" is enabled.
5. Next, select the Drawing | Line option.
6. Next, with the Line options active, select the front end point of the top reference line.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
7. Then the bottom end point of the back reference line.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 8. Now you can see you have your clip in place. So you can now get rid of the reference lines
      using the Modify | Delete option.

 9. To establish your new Part perimeter you will need to trim away the unnecessary portions of
      the Part's shape using the Modify | Trim Delete option.

10. Simply click the portions of the Part shape you do not need.

                                                                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
11. To confirm that your shape is fully enclosed select the Shape | Check Shape option. Notice
      after running Check Shape that all of the lines that make up the Part's perimeter are Green.
      This indicates the Part shape is complete with no errors and that you are good to go.

                                                                       © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
12. So now you have the basic shape of the part, you can click the Return option to Save it.
  Now you already have intelligence added to the parts, so that when the object is re-sized the parts
  will re-size themselves too. And, now you have just changed the shape on the middle part so that
  it looks like you want it to. So, now test everything by changing the size of the object and then look
  to see how everything reacts.
  Here is an example of what happens to the shape when you change the size of the Object. You
  can see that the 2" offset we wanted is not being held when you change the size of the Object. So
  you need to Constrain certain portions of the shape to prevent this from happening.

                                                                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
1. Return the Object to the standard size and return to the Assembly Level End Ortho View
    and then right click this part and select Edit.

add some Constraints to the Shaped Part.

We only need to add simple Constraints to the lines we wish to remain at 2".

3. Select the topmost 2" Line.

                                © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
4. For Start Y in the sidebar select the Lock Top option.
5. Select the bottommost 2" Line.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.

You can see here the Part is sized and shaped properly.

    "Wood Top" as the part type. Under the "Material" area it should have a panel stock material
    listed (some kind of Plywood would be perfect). Click on "Next".

8. In the "Size" window set the size of this part to 28.5"L and 23.25"W. Leave the thickness
    alone. This part is the main piece of the wood top and its length will be what ever the width of
    the cabinet is minus the thickness of the two end skirts. The width of this part is whatever the
    depth of the cabinet is minus the thickness of the front skirt. Click on "Next".

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 9. In the "Orientation" window leave the orientation set to "Front". Click on "Next".

10. In the "Finish" window check to see that the finish is set to "Exterior" for the front, back, and
      edges. Click on the "Finish" button.

  You will now be at a Face ortho view and in the sidebar the "Left/Right" will be "-15 inches".

 1. Set the "Left/Right" to .75 inches and press enter. This will move the part so that it is inside of
      the empty cabinet and leave room for the thickness of the left skirt.

  This part is going to be the main piece of our wood top. We are going to have to lay it face up with
  the grain running left to right. Also we will need to raise it up so that the face is flush with the top
  of the empty cabinet. If you click on this part from different ortho views you can see that the
  reference point is in the left, bottom, and back corner. In order to lay this piece face up with the
  grain running left to right, we are going to have to rotate this part on two different axis. First we
  will rotate the part so the face is facing up, and then we will rotate the part so that the grain is
  running left to right.

 2. In order to lay the wood top down so that the face is facing up it will be the X-axis that will act
      as a hinge. In order to face the reference point we will have to look at the part from an End
      ortho view. Click on the "End" ortho view and then click on the part. We want the part to lay
      face up so we will be rotating the part clockwise, we will be entering a negative amount. Enter
      -90 into the "Rotation" area and press enter.

 3. Now we will rotate the part so the grain is running left to right. In order to rotate the part so that
      the grain is running left to right and the reference point stays on the left side. It is the Y-axis
      that will be acting as a hinge and we will rotate the part clockwise so that the reference point
      stays on the left side. If we were to rotate the part counter-clockwise the reference point would
      be on the right end of the part. We will be entering a negative amount. Enter -90 into the
      "Rotation" area and press enter.

  Click on the part while in different ortho views, note where the reference point is, note where the
  part is. You will notice that it needs to be raised up to be flush with the top of the base object it is
  contained in.

 4. Click on the Face ortho view tab and then click on the part. In the sidebar, enter .75 in the "Up/
      Down" window.

  This piece is now rotated and placed correctly. Next we will add the left "Skirt".

  Adding the Left Skirt

 1. Click on the Face ortho view tab.

 2. Click on "New Part". In the "Part Type" area select "Skirt" as the part type. Under the
      "Material" area it should have a board stock listed (some kind of lumber would be perfect).
       Click on "Next".

                                                                        © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
3. In the "Size" window set the size of this part to 24"L and 1.5"W. Leave the thickness alone.
     This part is the left skirt of the wood top and its length will be what ever the depth of the
    cabinet is. We are going to let this piece and the front piece overlap each other, as we would
    most likely miter the side skirt into the front skirt if we were to build this wood top. The width of
    this part is whatever the height of the cabinet is. Click on "Next".
