    edges. Click on the "Finish" button.

You will now be at a Face ortho view and in the sidebar the "Left/Right" will be "-15 inches".

6. Set the "Left/Right" to 0" and press enter. This will move the part so that it is inside of the
    empty cabinet.

We now need to rotate this part so that the length is going front, to back, and the width is going up
and down. My first thought when rotating this part would be to rotate it on the Y-axis -90 (so the
face was pointing to the left) and then rotate it on the X-axis +90 so that it was lying down (with the
length running front to back). This would place the reference point in the right, top and back
corner. However when you rotate a part in an object (cabinet or another part), you always want to
try and keep the reference point as close to the left, bottom, and back corner of the object as you
can. As this will cut down on the number of placement formulas you have to write. Also it doesn't
really matter (in this case) if the back of this part is facing out, as the material is lumber.

There is a way to rotate this part so that it is rotated and placed to be the left skirt of our wood top,
and yet the reference point would remain in the left, bottom, and back corner.

7. See if you can rotate this part so that its reference point stays where it was when the part was
    brought in (The left, bottom, and back corner). And yet it is rotated in the correct direction. If
    you get the rotation really hosed up click on the "Remove Rotation" button and try again. If you
    get the rotation right you will not have to write any formulas for the placement of this part.

Answer

This part is now placed and rotated correctly. We are now ready to place the right hand skirt.
 Instead of adding a new part, we can just copy the part we have already placed.

Copying the Left Skirt to Make The Right Skirt

1. From the Face ortho view, right click on the left skirt and select "Copy", from the right click
    menu.

2. Move your mouse (and the phantom part) to the right and line it up with the right side of your
    wood top. See picture below. Then "Left Click" one time to "place" the part, and then "Right
    Click" one time to "release" the phantom part.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
3. Click on the right skirt. In the sidebar set the "Left/Right" to 29.25" (because of where the
    reference point is located the "Left/Right" (X) of this part is the thickness of the left skirt plus the
    length of the wood top, or the width of the cabinet minus the thickness of the right skirt).

4. Set the "Up/Down" to 0".

5. Set the "In/Out" to 0".

The right skirt is now placed and rotated correctly. Look at your wood top in 3D by clicking on the
3D view tab. As you can see we have correctly rotated and placed three of the four parts. We are
now ready to add the front skirt.

Adding The Front Skirt

1. Click on the Face ortho view tab.

2. Click on "New Part", in the "Part Type" area select "Skirt" as the part type, then click "Next".

3. In the "Size" window set the size of this part to 30"L and 1.5"W. Leave the thickness alone.
     This part is the front skirt of the wood top and its length will be what ever the width of the
    cabinet is. We are going to let this piece and the sidepieces overlap each other, as we would
    most likely miter the side skirts into the front skirt if we were to build this wood top. The width
    of this part is whatever the height of the cabinet is. Click on "Next".

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
4. In the "Orientation" window leave the orientation set to "Front". Click on "Next".

5. In the "Finish" window check to see that the finish is set to "Exterior" for the front, back, and
    edges. Click on the "Finish" button.

You will now be at the Face ortho view and in the sidebar the "Left/Right" will be "-15 inches".

1. Set the "Left/Right" to 0" and press enter. This will move the part so that it is inside of the
    empty cabinet.

2. As you can see the part is running up and down. We need to tip the part to the right so that the
    length is going from left to right. Click on the part and rotate it so that it is running from left to
    right. Remember to keep the reference point as close to where it was, as possible. Answer,
    enter -90 in the rotation.

3. As you can see, because of where the reference point is, this part is placed to low. Enter 1.5"
    in the "Up/Down" window and press enter. This part will be placed up and down (Y) at
    whatever the height of the cabinet happens to be.

4. If you look at the wood top from a 3D view by clicking on the 3D tab. You will notice that this
    part is in the back of the wood top. We want it to be in the front, so move it to the front.
     Answer; enter 23.25" in the "In/Out" window. Because of where the reference point for this
    part is located this part will be placed in and out (Z) at whatever the depth of the cabinet is
    minus the thickness of the front skirt, or whatever the width (DX) of the wood top is.

All the parts are now rotated and placed correctly, so we will now give them intelligence. Lets start
with the wood top, then the left skirt, then the right skirt and then the front skirt.

Sixth Exercise Notes on Formulas

In the section that follows, I want you to think about whether or not we need a formula for the
parameter in question. Do we? Think about it a little. What should happen to the parts if we
change the width, height or depth of the Wood Top? If you need help you can click on "Answer".

I want you to try and come up with the formula yourself. Think about how the parts are related to
the overall size of the Wood Top, and the other parts in the Wood Top. Click on each piece and
notice where the reference point is and how it relates to the reference point of the Wood Top (left,
bottom, and back corner). If you need help you can click on "Formula".

Once you have written down your formula, trace it through the tree to get the code and write the
code down. If you need help you can click on "Code".

I have purposely left out the step-by-step instructions for giving the parts intelligence; if you did the
five exercises up till now you should know the steps. If you need help refer to the section "Steps to
writing a Formula " in the first exercise.

There is more than one way to skin a cat, so you may come up with a different formula and code

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
than the samples shown here. If you do, try your code and see what happens. If it works, great!
Then compare it to what is shown here and see which one you like best.

What We Learned

 You should have noticed that any time the X, Y, or Z is equal to 0" you don't have to write a
   formula for the placement parameter.

 You should have noticed that we didn't write any formulas for the thickness of the parts, the
   thickness of the parts comes from the material the part is made from.

 You should have noticed that you didn't write any formulas for the AX, AY, or AZ. You almost
   never have to write a formula for the rotation because once a part is rotated into place it almost
   never changes rotation.

 You should have noticed that if you size and place the part correctly to start with, you are using
   the formulas you need to size and place the part.

Adding A List To A Label

There are times that a small list of information must be added to a label. You can do this using
CV's built in concat functionality.
What does concat mean?
When you concatenate (or concat for shorthand) a string, it means you are taking a variable
number of strings, like:
"Hello"
"World"
And putting them together into a single string:
"Hello World"
As an example, let's create the following view in Cabinet Vision:
DoorLabels
SELECT Doors.[Cabinet ID], Doors.[Label] + ' - ' + Doors.[Type] as DoorLabel
FROM Doors
For my database, that creates the following view in the Report.mdb:

Cabinet ID  DoorLabel
1           Open.1A - DF
1           1B-L - P
1           1B-R - P
2           Open.1A - DF
2           1B-L - P
2           1B-R - P
3           Open.1A - DF
3           1B-L - P

            © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
3           1B-R - P

4           Open.1A - DF

4           1B-L - P

4           1B-R - P

We can see that, in CABINET VISION, I have 4 cabinets that have 3 doors each (I basically
created a cabinet and copied it 3 times). Since labels can't create lists, we need to use this
feature to get what we want, which would look like this:

Cabinet ID  Door Label
1
2           Open.1A - DF
3           1B-L - P
4           1B-R - P

            Open.1A - DF
            1B-L - P
            1B-R - P

            Open.1A - DF
            1B-L - P
            1B-R - P

            Open.1A - DF
            1B-L - P
            1B-R - P

As you can now see, all items that have a related 'Cabinet ID' (meaning a 'Cabinet ID' that is the
same) have been combined, or rather concatenated, together into a single string that we can now
place on our label.

Step by Step:

1. Create a new report in CABINET VISION.

2. Right click on the Report and select Properties.

3. Create an 'Import'.

    a. Name: DoorLabels

    b. Type: Link

    c. SQL: SELECT Doors.[Cabinet ID], Doors.[Label] + ' - ' + Doors.[Type] as DoorLabel FROM
        Doors

            © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
4. Create a new table.
    a. Make this a cabinets table.
    b. On the comment list, select the following:
         i. Primary Field: Cabinet ID
        ii. Foreign Table: DoorLabels
       iii. Foreign Field: Cabinet ID
        iv. Display Field: DoorLabels

Now, when you run your report, you will have a new variable, that is in a sub-folder of the table's
folder, with your door labels, that allow you to place this list on the label.

from within CABINET VISION most Tables within Report.mdf are flushed and re-populated.

MaterialOverride

This table will contain either the Waste from the Material Catalog or the Waste recalculated using
the area of the parts and the number of sheets used in Optimization. The waste values will change
anytime a filter is applied. Since we are adjusting the Waste Factor the material totals per cabinet
will be in a ratio to the number of sheets used (not an even number of sheets). You can get the
number of sheets for a single cabinet by applying a filter for that cabinet (or any combination).

Door Sizing

Door sizing refers to the overall size of a finished Door, not to the dimensions of the individual
parts of the Door. If you are searching for information on dimensioning of the component Parts,
see the Door Manager.

Doors are sized in two ways, depending on the Construction Style of the Assembly.

For Face Frame Cabinets, the Doors are sized according to the following formula.

Clear opening of the Face Frame + Door Overlay = Door size. Drawer Fronts adopt the
same Overlay as the Door.

              © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Overlay is a property of a Hinge. As such, it is found on the Hinge Tab for the Hinge in the Material
Manager. A single Door that was to cover a 20 inch by 20 inch Face Frame opening, using a Hinge
with a 1/2 inch overlay, would produce a Door that was 21 inches by 21 inches.
32 millimeter, Frameless, Closet 32mm, and Frame Overlay Style Assemblies do not use overlay
to size Doors. These Assemblies look to the values you have entered in the Assembly Wizard for
Reveals to determine the Door and Drawer face size. The formula for sizing these Doors is as
follows:
Overall Assembly dimension - Reveals = Door Size(s).
A 20" (overall dimension) Assembly with 1/8 inch reveals all around, would produce a 19 3/4 inch
by 19 3/4 inch Door.
Steps to Creating a Door
1. Select the Category where you want your Door.
2. Click on New.
3. Name the Door and give it a Description.
4. Select the Door Type.
5. Click Finish.
Shaping the Top or Bottom Rail
To shape the Top or Bottom Rail.
1. Make sure the Rail is the correct size.
2. In the Door Editor (Section) right click on the Rail and select "Edit Shape".

If you only want the picture to look good and you don't care if the parts are right you can just select

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
"Arch". Casebuilder will arch the Door for you. However the Parts might not be correct.
Right clicking on the rail and selecting "Edit Shape" will bring you to the Shape Editor. Your screen
should look something like below. See The Shape Editor topic for more information on the Shape
Editor tools.

Inside Edge Profiles
If you are making your own Doors, what an Inside Edge Profile is, and what it does, is an
important concept to understand. The shape of the inside edge cut is not as important as the
depth/width of the cut. This is because the shape of the Inside Edge cut is merely decorative while
the depth/width of the cut can be used by CABINET VISION to size your door parts.

               If you are making a Door with a frame around it and you are using cope & stick
       construction for the Door, you will not be able to get your Door parts to size correctly until
       you have selected an Inside Edge Profile to use with that Door that has a "width" equal to
       the "depth" of your Door cutters. This is because Solid can add the width of the Inside Edge
       Profile to each end of the Top Rail, Mid Rail, Bottom Rail, and any Mid Stiles, for the cope &
       stick.
CABINET VISION comes preset with some sample Inside Edge Profiles. However if you can't find
one in the list, that matches the depth/width of your Door cutters. You will need to create your own

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
  that does match the depth/width of your Door cutters before you will be able to get your Door parts
  to size correctly.
  When creating Door Profiles the Inside Edge Profile has a property called Applied. What you have
  set here determines whether the Inside Edge Profile will affect the width of your Stiles and Rails or
  not.

Overview of Editing Assemblies

An understanding of the Hierarchy of CABINET VISION is necessary before you will fully appreciate the
editing potential of CABINET VISION. Assembly Editing requires an understanding of the various
areas that editing is possible, as well as which areas allow for Assemblies or Parts to retain their
logic (I.E., stretch, etc). Editing is the process of sectioning an Assembly or object so that it
acquires the look and status of the new Assembly. Typically, this is accomplished by two methods
of editing. Section editing is the process where an Assembly is divided into vertical or horizontal
areas that are assigned properties, such as Door, Drawer, or Roll Out. Orthographic editing is the
process of adding or replacing Parts, and thereafter re-establishing intelligence, or allowing an
Override on that Part to exist. These two methods also represent the two main editing views:

Section Editing - This allows for intelligent editing of the Face and interior (Case) of an Assembly.
This also includes menu options for rapidly changing Assembly Properties and attributes. Section
Editing is the favored method of Assembly editing. It allows for modifications to the Assembly
Face as well as the Assembly interior (Case). All editing performed in the Section Editing views
retains intelligence with the Assembly. The retention of intelligence allows the edited Part or area
to respond to changes in an Assemblies dimensions. Access to the "Section Face" view is gained

via the Section  tab, and the Section Face  option.

                 © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
The Section Interior option is typical to the above graphic, with the exception that the Section

Interior  option is selected while in the section window, the Section                 tab must be

clicked before either the "Section Face" or "Section Interior" Section tools appear.

Section Editing is a feature of the Assembly Level of CABINET VISION. Therefore the changes
you are making to the Assembly in this level are limited to that Assembly, and will not appear on
other Assemblies within that Room. If you desire the changes to be available for additional
Assemblies, consider saving the Assembly to your library.

Access Via the "Section" View Menu Option

Another method that allows section editing of an Assembly and has as an additional feature; the
Elevation from which the Assembly exists at shown, is the "Section" option available at the
"Layout" level. Access this option by right clicking on an Assembly in the Elevation View of the
Layout Level, and select the menu option "Section". You will then be able to Section Edit the
Assembly live in the Elevation View without having to go to the Assembly Level.

Orthographic Editing - This editing is the more powerful of the two, at the expense of possible logic
being lost. Overrides on Part logic can occur here too. See the section on Orthographic Editing,

          © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
and the section on overrides for more information.

Section Face/Section Interior Logic Transfer

CABINET VISION has a feature that will apply logic from the face of an Assembly to the interior of
the Assembly for specific items. These items are similar for face frame and frameless design. The
following Parts are recipients of logic from the design of the Assembly Face. Drawer Stretchers,
Partitions, and Fixed Shelves. Typically, an Assembly needs a Partition behind two Doors or
behind a Mid Stile. It may be desirable that this Partition follow the reveal between the Doors or
the Mid Stile as the Doors change Widths. The Partition can be given logic from the Doors to
follow their dimensions by using the following procedure.
Section the face of the Assembly, here two single Doors were added to the face of the Assembly
(not a pair of Doors). After the Doors were added, the Section Interior option was clicked. The
graphic below is from the Section Interior view. Note the position of the Mid Stile.

In order to give the Partition logic to the Doors, click on the Split Opening Vertically tool without
highlighting any portion of the case. After clicking on the tool, click somewhere inside the outline of
the Mid Stile. View the side bar to determine the Relative Position placement as "Left", "Right" or
"Center". Click on each of these options and the Partition will move accordingly.
The procedure is similar for all Parts that receive logic from the face.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Multiple Faces

It is quite simple to add additional faces to an Assembly using the side selector in the Section
Editor. The side selector appears in the sidebar of the Section Editor when no Parts of the
Assembly have been selected (NOTE: The side selector is not available when you are editing in
one of the orthographic views). If you do not see the side selector, simply click somewhere outside
of the Assembly itself in the white space that surrounds it.

The side selector represents a plan type view of the Assembly that you are editing and the current
side appears as a red line. The other sides of the Assembly appear as dotted lines. To edit one of
the other sides of the Assembly, simply click on that side in the side selector and you will see that
the Section Editor will then show that side and it will also appear as a red line in the side selector.
Notice that in the screen below I have clicked on the right side of the Assembly in the side selector
and so that side appears in the Section Editor. Also notice that the right side in the side selector is
now appearing in red.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
You now have the option to choose any end type for the selected side of the Assembly.
When you want to change an existing end to a face, simply click the Face radio button under Side
Types (see below).

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
When you have more than one face on an Assembly, the side selector will show a number next to
each face. This number is the priority ranking of that face. The face priority controls how the
internal parts of the Assembly react to each other.

For example: A partition that is placed in the face with priority of 1 (the Highest Priority) will go
through the entire Assembly while the Partition placed from the face with priority of 2 will end
when it comes in contact with the priority 1 Partition. Below is a view looking down into an
Assembly with 2 faces with a Partition in each face. Notice the way that the Partitions meet due to
the face priorities.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
And below is the same Assembly with the face priorities switched....

Editing Assembly Interiors

Editing of the Assembly interior is independent of the Assembly face. The face does not
necessarily effect the interior as it is edited. Always check the Assembly interior after editing the
face to insure your needs are met. Be sure to check out the topic on Logic Transfer for information
about how to relate the interior Parts to the face sectioning.

To change from face to interior view, select the "Section Interior" option. Both the Section view tab
and the Section Interior option must be used to access this option.

The same 4 editing tools are available, Single and Multiple, Horizontal and Vertical division
options. When editing the interior of an Assembly, the interior area where the item is to be added
is selected, and the appropriate edit tool is clicked. Here an Adjustable Shelf is added. To select
the Shelf that we have just added to the Assembly, simply click on it. With the Shelf highlighted in

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
red, the appropriate dot is clicked at the left, here Adjustable Shelf was clicked, thus, an
Adjustable Shelf has been added. It could just as easily have been a Roll Out tray.

Vertical Divisions are done in the same manner, however, they produce Partitions instead of
Shelves.
Deleting Shelves, Trays, etc.
Items that you have added via the method shown in this topic, can be deleted by highlighting and
clicking the large red "X" tool located next to the section face and section case tools. Assembly
Parts can not be deleted this way. To delete Assembly Parts, use the Hide Parts menu option under
the Modifications option.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Tips and Tricks

Remember, it is always a good idea to edit an Assembly that has been stretched, shrunk, etc., to
the correct size.

On editing the interior, much like the exterior, the order in which you edit will determine which
Parts run long or split. Regardless of how you have set up any Construction Method, the order that
you divide the Assembly interiors determines which Part(s) are long, and which are short. An
example would be where a long Partition was desired, with Shelves on each side of the Partition.
If the Partition is created before the Shelves, all is well, however, if the Shelves are created before
the Partition is created, the Partition will be split by the long Shelves, regardless of how you have
defined your Construction Method.

See the topic on Transferring Logic from Face parts to Case parts.

Consider "defaulting" your Assembly before editing it. This has the advantage of eliminating the
interior members, and the face members. It allows editing a basic "box" that can be rebuilt to meet
your needs.

Objects In CABINET VISION

CABINET VISION has many objects; Rooms, Walls, Assemblies, Decks, Stiles and Rails are all
objects in CABINET VISION. Each of these objects are very similar. The object's type and
parameters make it unique, a parameter is a characteristic or attribute of an object. Although
almost every object has the basic 9 parameters, typically objects have more than the standard
nine.

The Basic 9 Parameters

The basic 9 parameters describe where an object sits in space.

 X, Y and Z are position points.

 DX, DY, and DZ are dimensions

 AX, AY, and AZ are axis of rotation.

 X = Position on X Axis

 Y = Position on Y Axis

 Z = Position on Z Axis

 DX = Width

 DY = Length / Height (Part / Wall)

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 DZ = Thickness / Depth (Part / Wall)
 AX = Rotation on X Axis
 AY = Rotation on Y Axis
 AZ = Rotation on Z Axis

Position X, Y, Z

 The coordinates of a Part are in reference to its point of origin.
 The coordinates of the Part in the diagram above are x=0, y=0 and z=0.
 The coordinates of the diagram to the left are x=60, y=52, and z=0. These coordinates are in

   reference to the start of the Wall.
 The X position moves a point of origin right (+) and left (-).
 The Y position moves a point of origin up (+) and down (-).
 The Z position moves a point of origin forward (+) and backward (-).

Dimension DX, DY, DZ

 DX can be thought of as the width for a Part or the width of Assemblies and Walls.
 DY can be thought of as the length for a Part or the height of Assemblies and Walls.
 DZ can be thought of as the thickness for a Part or the depth of Assemblies and Walls.

Axis of Rotation AX, AY, AZ
Right Hand Rule

The right-hand rule determines the positive axis direction of the Z axis when you know the
direction of the X and Y axes in a 3D coordinate system. The right-hand rule also determines the
positive rotation direction about an axis in 3D space.

To determine the positive axis direction of the X, Y, and Z axes, place the back of your right hand

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
near the screen. Point your thumb in the direction of the positive X axis. Extend your index and
middle fingers as illustrated and point your index finger in the direction of the positive Y axis. Your
middle finger indicates the direction of the positive Z axis.
 Thumb = X axis
 Index finger = Y axis
 Middle finger = Z axis
 Looking towards the point of origin of each axis, clockwise is (-) negative, and counterclockwise

   is (+) positive.
 Order of rotation of a Part is X, then Y, then Z.
 The axis does not move with the Part.
 Example #1: An Adjustable Shelf rotates on the X-axis (AX=-90) and then on the Y-axis

   (AY=-90). If the axis moved with the Part the rotation would have been (AX = -90), (AZ = -90).
 Example #2: For an angled Shelf it would be nice to describe as (AX = -90, AY = -90, AX = 15)

   or (AX = -75, AY = -90). The correct rotation is (AY = -75, AZ = -90). Use the rotation tool in
   CABINET VISION when you are having difficulty.

Building Orientation

 Every Part is built the same way. A Rail, Stile, Left End, Right End, Door or Drawer Box Bottom.
 All Parts are built with the same orientation and then moved into place.
 In the diagram there is an example of a Rail and how the building orientation differs from the

   coordinates once it is placed on a Assembly.

Object Tree

Concept

 The Object Tree is just another way to view the data in CABINET VISION.
 The tree consists of objects, parameters, and values or equations for those parameters.
 A great way to view the structure of the Job and understand the inner workings of CABINET

   VISION.
 Select the Object Tree tab from the bottom of the sidebar.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Coordinates Are In Relation To Their Parents

 All X, Y, Z positions are in reference to their parents.
 A Rail on a Assembly has an X = 3, Y = 34, and Z = 24. These coordinates are in reference to

   its parent, the Assembly.

Modifying Parameters

 All parameter values can be modified.
 Virtually anything modified through the normal means in CABINET VISION can also be modified

   through the Object Tree.

Example of Modifying Parameters in the Layout View

 Click on the individual Assembly that needs to be modified and the sidebar contains values for
   the depth, width, and length of the Assembly.

 These are the DX, DY, and DZ values.
 Manually edit the parameters of the Assembly by clicking in the spaces and modifying the

   value.

Example of Modifying Parameters in the Object Tree

 Go to the layout view of CABINET VISION.
 Click the Object Tree tab from the bottom of the sidebar.
 Open the tree (click on the plus signs) until you find the Part that needs to be modified.
 Click on Top Stretcher. Notice at the right all the parameters for the TS are available.
 Click on DY to edit the length of the Part. The edit button will become available after DY is

   highlighted.
 Click on Edit.
 Manually enter the modified value for DY.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
© 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Notice back in the Layout view that the length of the Top Stretcher (TS) has changed.

Equations - From Simple to Advanced
Introduction

 Equations can be used as parameter values.
 In a simple equation a directional operator or operators are found paired with key words.
 A key word is a term or header that is found in the Object Tree.
 Combining directional operators and key words allow you to access other parameters in the

   Object Tree.

Levels

 A level in the Object Tree is one grouping. Think of the tree being divided into quadrants. Each
   quadrant line that is crossed is another level of the tree.

Directional Operators

 Directional operators allow you to move around the tree. A colon (:) moves up the tree one
   level. A period (.) drops down a level in the tree.

Key Words

 Key words are special headings in the Object Tree that allow quick access to a position in the
   tree. See the example below:

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Exercise

 In the following tree, visualize the divisions from left to right that would be in the tree.
 To reference a parent use the (:) operator.
 To reference a child use the (.) operator.
 No operator is required to reference a sibling.
 The letters in bold represent key words.
 When multiple types of the same Assembly are in the Object Tree there must be a special term

   used to define it. In the example Object Tree below there are three J's. Each J has its own
   parameters; however, each of them is named differently by their position. Use the @ operator to
   reference an object that has siblings of the same name. This is commonly seen when a
   Assembly has multiple Shelves.

Creating Smart Parts

 When a Part is added to a Assembly it is considered a dumb Part. You can adjust the Part to
   the correct size and position, but as the Assembly changes the Part doesn't.

 The problem we ran into with the new parameters of the TS was when the Assembly
   parameters were increased or decreased the TS did not have the smarts to adjust with the

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
   Assembly.
 The purpose in having equations is to expand the flexibility of Parts in CABINET VISION. By

   using an equation we can modify a parameter and reference it to the Assembly so in the case
   that the Assembly is modified the Part will be smart and justify itself also.
 If a smart Part already exists in CABINET VISION and its parameters are similar to the
   new Part, use the parameters in the equation instead of writing a brand new equation.
 Key words are used to automatically access a position in the tree.
 It is best not to enter in hard code numbers when dealing with equations. Giving parameters as
   boundaries versus actual numeric dimension will allow for that flexibility.

Example: Adding a Smart Top Stretcher
Prepare The Assembly

 Let us begin by preparing the Assembly. Place a Std Base on the Wall then edit it at the
   Assembly level. From the Section view select the option Properties | Case. Then change the
   Top Type to No Top.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Select one of the Ortho Views        tabs.

Add The Part

 Select the sidebar button New Part.

 Select the Part type Top Stretcher. If you do not adjust the Material with the change button this
   will cause the Part's Material to be linked to the same Material as a Top Stretcher. The Top
   Stretcher's Material is defined in the Assembly's Material Schedule. When the Material
   Schedule for this Assembly changes - this Part's Material will change automatically. If you
   wanted to Lock this Part to a Particular Material, you could select the Material with the change
   button.

 Select Next >. Then make the Length of the Top Stretcher 24" and the width of the top stretcher
   4". This is just an initial size. We will be writing equations to change it.

                                                                    © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Select Next >. Select a Part orientation of Top. This will rotate the Part to the proper orientation.

                                                                    © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Select Next >. Then select the finish properties for the Part. Make the top and back face out of
   the interior finish and the edges from the exterior finish.

                                                                    © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Select Finish.

Write Equation For Parts Length

 Now select the Part in each of the Ortho  Views. Take note that the Part's

reference point, the blue-green dot when the Part is selected, is in the bottom, back, left corner

of the Part.

 We will begin by writing equations to size the Part. Then we will concentrate on setting the
   Part's position. Let us make some assumptions about this Assembly. First, that the deck will
   always exist in the Assembly and second that the Top Stretcher's length will always be same as
   the deck length. With this assumption, you can change the deck/end construction from a butt
   joint to a dado, and the top stretcher will adjust right along with it.

 There is no need to make this assumption. The Part can be setup independently from the deck
   however making assumptions like this will make your equations more flexible in the end.

 Click the Object Tree tab in the sidebar and expand the tree as shown.

              © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Highlight the DY parameter and select Edit. Change from a Value to an Equation.

                                                                    © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 The computer will use the THEN (equation) when the value of the IF (condition) is not 0. By
   entering a 1 as the condition, we are telling the computer to always use this equation.

 For the equation we will enter Case.DE.DY, this can be read as "The length of the deck in the
   case". This will ensure that the Top Stretcher will always have the same length as the deck.
   Now we can select the Test Equation button. Note the value.

 If there were a spelling error in the equation, the result would be ERROR. You would then need
   to correct the error and select Test again.

                                                                    © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Notice that as soon as you click OK on for the Parameter the Part snaps to the same length of
   the deck.

 As we modify the size of the Assembly we can see the Stretcher adjusting size with it.
 Notice that if we modify the scribe or height of the Assembly the Part is only "Smart" for the

   parameter that has an equation.

Equation for Parts X Position

 Return to the Object Tree and select the X parameter of the top stretcher.
 Once again we will reference the deck in our equation. We will set the Top Stretchers X position

   equal to the Decks X position. Enter an equation of Case.DE.X this can be read as "The X
   position of the deck in the case".

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Equation for Parts Y Position

 We will reference the Parts Y position of the Assembly.
 Select the Y parameter and add the equation: Cab.DY or :DY
 As we exit the Parameter we see that the Stretcher is actually hovering above our Assembly.

                         The origin of the Part is at the bottom of the Part. Therefore we must account
                  for the Part thickness in our equation.
 Return the Y parameter and modify the equation to Cab.DY - DZ this can be translated as the
   height of the Assembly minus the Parts thickness.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Equation for Parts Z Position

 The equation for the Z position of the stretcher will be very similar to the Y position. Taking into
   account that the reference point for the stretcher is in the back, left, bottom corner, we want the
   Z position of the stretcher to be: The depth of the Assembly, minus the stretcher width.

 In this equation we will reference an object in the Assembly tree that is not a Part or Assembly.
   We will be referencing the Face of the Assembly.

 The Face, Case, & Interior are special objects in the Assembly that serve as containers for
   other objects and Parts.

 The Face object contains the Assemblies Face Frame, Doors and Drawers.

 By writing our equation referencing the Face of the Assembly, rather than the Assembly itself,
   we automatically account for the face frame.

 Follow the same steps as before selecting the Z parameter of the stretcher. Once again, we will
   enter 1 for the IF condition. Now enter the following equation. Face.Z - DX. This can be read as
   the Z position of the face minus the width of the Top Stretcher. This will take into account that
   the point of origin is in the back of the stretcher.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Equation for Parts Width

 Select the DX Parameter for the Top Stretcher. Select the Edit button. Select the Equation
   option then select Add.

 This time we will be entering something other then 1 for the IF condition. By default, we
   would like this stretcher to be 4" wide. However on occasion we might want it to be 3" or 8".
   Since the width may change, we are going to say it is equal to a variable TS_WIDTH. We can
   set a value for this variable so that the Part will adjust dynamically as the value for the variable
   changes. At the same time, we do not want the burden of having to add a custom parameter to
   each job since most of the time this Part will be 4" wide. To accomplish this we are going to
   enter a parameter for the condition and a parameter for the equation.

 Enter TS_WIDTH for the condition and TS_WIDTH for the equation. The statement can be read
   as follows. If there is a parameter named TS_WIDTH, and the value of TS_WIDTH is not equal
   to 0, make the width of the Part the value of TS_WIDTH.

 If you select Test you will get an error in the test result Syntax Error. This is normal since at this
   time the parameter named TS_WIDTH does not exist in the tree.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Now we will set the default width for the stretcher to 4".
 Select the Add button again. Then enter 1 for the condition and 4 for the equation. Then Select

   OK.

                                                                    © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 The Parameter Edit Dialog Box should look something like the screen above. We have entered
   two equations for the width of this Part. One is based on a parameter. The other is a default
   value.

 When there are multiple equations for a Part, the equations are evaluated one by one
   until a condition is not equal to 0. In the example above if the TS_WIDTH equation returns a
   false answer CABINET VISION immediately evaluates the next formula which is 4".

Equation for Parts Thickness

 No equation is needed for a Parts thickness. The material it is made out of determines the
   Parts thickness. Therefore, the thickness of a Part is automatically smart.

 Our Part is completely defined. Go ahead and modify the size of the Assembly. You will see that
   the Part will move and stretch exactly as we have defined it.

Adding Custom Parameters To A Job

 Now we will demonstrate how to set parameters in a Job and have our Part adjust with those
   parameters. Return to the Layout (Room) Level and add a second Wall to the job. Then go to
   the Object Tree. If you expand the Object Tree, you will see it contains all objects in this room.
   Select Wall 2 and select the New Parameter button to add a parameter.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Change the Style to an Attribute.
 For the Name enter TS_WIDTH.
 For the Description enter Top Stretcher Width:
 Enter 2 for the parameters value. Then select OK.

                                                                    © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Now we will repeat the procedure for the back face of Wall #2. Highlight the back face of Wall
   #2. Add a parameter named TS_WIDTH with a value of 8. Then close the Object Tree.

 Back at the Plan view of the Layout (Room) Level, copy the Assembly. Place one copy on the
   front face of Wall #2 and a second copy on the back face of Wall #2. Then select the 3-D
   perspective view and observe the various top stretcher widths.

How CABINET VISION Searches for Parameters

 When a parameter is found in an equation CABINET VISION looks to see if the parameter
   exists for that object. If not it looks to see if the parameter exists in the parent of that object and
   so on until it gets to the top of the tree. All three Assemblies have the same equations for the
   top stretcher yet all three top stretchers are different sizes.

 The Assembly on Wall #1 looks to find the parameter TS_WIDTH. It does not exist at the Part
   level, Assembly level, Wall face level, Wall level, or room level. Therefore, it goes to the next
   equations IF 1 THEN 4 and the stretcher width is set to 4" wide.

 The Assembly on Wall #2's face looks to find the parameter TS_WIDTH. It does not exist at the
   Part level, Assembly level, Wall face level, but it does exist at the Wall level where the
   TS_WIDTH = 2. Therefore, the stretcher becomes 2" wide.

 The Assembly on Wall #2's back looks to find the parameter TS_WIDTH. It does not exist at the

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
   Part level, Assembly level, but it does exist at the Wall face level where the TS_WIDTH = 8.
   Therefore, the stretcher becomes 8" wide.

                         If we continued to search up the tree we would find the TS_WIDTH = 2 at the
                  Wall level, however once the 1st TS_WIDTH is found CABINET VISION stops
                  looking.

 This gives you tremendous flexibility with your equations. You can set a value at the room level,
   but you can "override" that value at the Wall, Wall face, Assembly, Part, or any level in the tree
   and your Parts can re-size dynamically. To further test this, move the Assembly on Wall #1 to
   Wall #2 and see how the top stretcher changes size.

Parameters in CABINET VISION

See Parameters and Functions

Where Are Parameters Stored

 All parameters in CABINET VISION are stored as high up in the tree as possible.

 This method allows for one parameter to effect many objects.

 It also allows a convenient way to store an override to an object.

 This method uses the least amount of memory. It leaves a small footprint. If a job has 20
   Assemblies in a single room. The information for the top rail would be stored 20 times for that
   same Part at the Part level. This would increase the size of the jobs exponentially.

 The Top Rail is found under the Parts list of a Assembly in the Object Tree. You might assume
   that the parameters or information about the Part is stored at the Part level. Actually, most of its
   parameters are stored much higher in the tree. Only the basic 9 parameters are stored for each
   Part.

 General info is stored at the Job Level. When starting a new job in CABINET VISION there are
   questions or parameters that need to be designated. These are the parameters that will be
   stored in the Job Level.

 CABINET VISION has four places to make overrides without using the Object Tree:

  1. Job Level

  2. Room Level

  3. Assembly Level

  4. Part Level

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Only minimal information is stored for each object.
 Every piece of information that a Part cannot find at its own home will travel up the tree until it

   finds the answer it is looking for.
 If a Part cannot find the information it is looking for it will return result of 0 for that parameter.

Demonstrate an Equation Based On Toe Height

 In this example we will write some sample equations based on the Toe Height for the Assembly.
   We will use 2 advanced methods to do so:
   1. First we will access a value from the Construction Method.
   2. Next we will reference a parameter in CABINET VISION.

 Lets continue to modify the Top Stretcher & write a new equation for the width of the Part.
 We will make the width of the Top Stretcher equal to the Toe Kick Height.
 Select the DX parameter of the Top Stretcher and enter the equation IF 1 THEN TOEH.

 When we exit the Object Tree we can see that the stretcher has disappeared. Actually TOEH

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
   was not found in the tree so the result returned 0 making the Width = 0.
 Modify the Toe Height of the Assembly from the section view and the Stretcher will reappear

   and equal the Toe Height.
 Like many parameters TOEH is only present if there is an override on the Assembly. Normally

   the Assembly references the Toe Height based on a standard in the current construction
   method.
 Launch the Assembly Manager. Start the wizard for the Toe Kick and look at the title Toe Kick
   Height: [Standard #238].

 Note the standard number: #238. We can reference this value in our equation.
 Return to the Object Tree and add the following equation to the DX parameter of the Top

   Stretcher. If 1 Then _CV:238. This formula can be read as Make the width of the stretcher equal
   to the Value entered for Construction Method Standard #238 (Toe Kick Height).

User Created Standards

Purpose

 The purpose of User Created Standards is to apply logic that is not controlled through the
   Assembly Wizard or any other Part of the program.

 This allows you to create smart Parts that are specific to your needs.
 You can create these smart Parts by one of the following methods:

  1. Add a brand new object
  2. Modify an object
  3. Delete an Object
 The power of UCS lies behind the interface-created macro, which can be put into its own
   language similar to Microsoft Visual BasicTM.

A Global View of UCS's

 UCS's provide a way to apply global changes to a job.
 Earlier an equation was written for a single Part in a Assembly. UCS's allow the same Part to

   have the same values for all Assemblies.
 UCS's also allow Parts to have the same value for similar Assemblies. Using a filter (Filters will

   be addressed later).

Accessing User Created Standards

 There are two ways to gain access to User Created Standards. The first way is from the
   welcome screen of CABINET VISION. The other way is from inside a job.

 Either way you access User Created Standards, the standards will be for all jobs.
 To access UCS's, start CABINET VISION. At the System Level, (the opening screen) select

   Utilities | User Created Standards.
 UCS's may be edited from within a job. To do this, double click on the Assembly. You can also

   right click and select Edit from the drop-down menu. Select any one of the
   three orthographic views. Again, select Utilities | User Created Standards. You will now see
   the UCS screen.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
The Screen Layout

 To add a User Created Standard, select the New option in the ribbonbar.

General Tab

 Notice, at the top of the User Created Standards window, that there are category tabs. These
   tabs are the steps that the titlebar is referring to. There are more tabs to the right that can be
   viewed by selecting the scroll arrow at the right of the screen.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 The first thing you're going to want to do is to give the UCS a name.

 By default, the standard type is Add. Select the type appropriate for the UCS you are writing. I
   am choosing to modify a Part.

Link to Tab

 The Link To tab will allow you to add or link an item to a specific Assembly, Part, or Operation.
   Depending on which one you select, your window to the right will display different selections.
   Review the groups and their associated selections and pick the most appropriate selection for
   your User Created Standard.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Assembly Class Tab

 This tab is the beginning of your ability to limit (filter) this User Created Standard to apply only in
   certain cases. Should you not want to limit to a specific Assembly class, select nothing here. If
   you need the standard to apply only on a certain class of Assembly, or object type, check only
   those for which you need the UCS to apply.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Assembly Properties Tab

 The Assembly Properties Tab will allow you the ability to establish which Assemblies will be
   available for a parameter to be effective. Currently, the default is all Assemblies, with no
   parameters.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Should you want to limit to a single Assembly, place the name in the field to the right of
   Assembly Name.

 Instead of limiting the standard to a single Assembly, maybe you want it to include multiple
   Assemblies in a grouping. Therefore you can use wild cards. The acceptable wild cards are the
   asterisk (*), or the question mark (?).

 As an example, std* will include any Assembly name that starts with std, regardless of any
   amount of characters after the std.

 The question mark replaces characters in a name. For example, having a Assembly name such
   as B?? will include all Assemblies with 2 characters after the letter B. B12, B48, etc. will be
   included in the grouping.

 Parameters will allow the User Created Standard to take affect only if the parameters that are
   checked meet the criteria based on the operation selected and the value that has been placed
   in the value field. Again, we are continuing with additional filters for the User Created
   Standards.

 An example of this would be setting up the depth of a Assembly to be greater than 12 inches
   before this standard would take affect.

                                                                    © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
End Types Tab

 The next filter is the end type of the Assembly. You can pick any end type for either end. Should
   you pick nothing, the default for that is all ends.

 You are able to pick virtually any combination of end types for this standard. To do that, select
   the appropriate end type for the left and right ends. Select the Add -> Button. Repeat this
   selecting the different end combinations until all your combinations are covered.

Construction Method Tab

 We can limit this standard to a single construction method, all construction methods or anything
   in between.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 By default, as with all the others, nothing marked means that there are no restrictions. Selecting
   one or all but one will then restrict this standard to only the construction methods selected.

Conditions for Object Tab

 This filter requires the object that is being linked to, not the new object being linked, meet
   certain conditions before the standard will take affect. Again, if nothing is selected, the default is
   no restrictions. If your modifying or deleting a Part then this tab is for you to set the conditions
   for the actual Part that is being modified or deleted.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 Notice the X Axis Rot, Y Axis Rot, and Z Axis Rot. These are there to allow you additional
   restrictions based on how the Part is oriented in space.

Part Values Tab

 The next tab, the Part Values tab allows you to establish the size of the Part you are linking. You
   can set a fixed value. You can set a value based on any dimension of the Part you're linking to.
   That Part, the Part your linking to is called the parent by CABINET VISION.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Part Parameters Tab

 The Part Parameters tab will allow you to add parameters to the Part such as additional Parts
   (QTY), repeating the item (REPT), or a spacing of a set of holes being bored (SPCNG). You can
   also type out any other Parameter you wish here.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 QTY will give an additional quantity of the Part especially if you're linking to another Part. An
   example of this could be setting the QTY to 4 if the Part was shelf pins and you would be linking
   to adjustable shelf.

 REPT could be used if you were adding 3 shelf holes in an end of a Assembly.
 SPCNG could be used to space the shelf holes if you were adding multiple shelves in an upper

   Assembly.
 You are not limited to just the three parameters that are listed. You can add any parameter you

   want. A word of warning though. If there is a parameter that is already set for this Part or
   operation, then this will replace that parameter. Be sure this is what you want to do.

Re-Open A User Created Standard

 Use the Wizard option to get back into a User Created Standard to change the parameters that
   you have set up.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 If you are going to change the parameters, be sure to use the Wizard option. Using this option
   with the correct User Created Standard highlighted will allow you to go back through the tabs
   that were discussed above. You can go directly to a parameter simply by clicking on the tab you
   need.
                               Use the Wizard option, to change your Standard not the Code option. The
                         Code option is used to change, or add to the logic that the User Created
                         Standard has already set up.

Organizing the User Created Standards

 Should you have to make multiple User Created Standards that are essentially the same but for
   some minor differences, use this option to copy the standard. Use the Wizard option to get into
   the standard to make the changes.

 You may decide you don't want a standard, or it has become unnecessary because the design
   you used it for is complete. Simply highlight the standard and click on the Delete option. The
   standard will be deleted from the list.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 CABINET VISION uses User Created Standards as they are listed. At times it is advantageous
   to have one standard acted upon before another standard. That's what the Up and Down
   buttons are used for.

 To use either button, highlight the User Created Standard you want to move. Click on the
   appropriate tool. The User Created Standard will be moved either up in priority or down in
   priority, depending on which tool you've selected.

 By right clicking your mouse on a User Created Standard, you have some of the same
   selections alternatively.

Advanced User Created Standards

 For those advanced users the Code option offers tremendous power to CABINET VISION.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
 For even greater flexibility, you have the ability to modify the code. You are able to access the
   computer-generated code CABINET VISION has created. From the choices you made when
   you answered the questions, programming code has been added. You can modify and add to
   that code. This ability gives great power to User Created Standards. Now nothing is
   unattainable for you.

User Created Standard Syntax
Comment ;

 Any text following a ; is ignored.

                      The 1st line of every UCS must be a comment.

For Each Object(s) ObjectType

 Multiple object names can be listed here with a | symbol to separate. Also wild card characters
   (*,?) may be used in the object names. Any parameters specified in the formula that are not
   proceeded with a . or : refer to the For Each Object(s).

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
The Filter - If & Then & End If

 A series of conditional statements that will filter out the UCS affecting every object. If the IF
   statement evaluates False the program flow drops to the corresponding End If statement. Some
   of the common items to filter on would be:
    Assembly Class
                      Cab.Class = ASM_CLASS_BASE
     Assembly Type
                      Cab.Type = ASM_TYPE_CORNER45
     Assembly Name
                      Cab.Name = 'BD*'
     Assembly Parameters
                      Cab.DX = 0
     Assembly End Types
                      Cab.REnd = ASM_END_CLIPPED and RClip > 0
     Construction ID
                      Cab.ConstID = 15
     Object Parameters
                      DX > 15

Modifying Parameters

 Following the If statements you can specify new parameters for the object. If the parameter
   does not exist it will be added. If the parameter does exist its value will be replaced. Following
   are some special parameter settings:
    QTY = 0 This will delete the object
    Adjust Add (X) This will add X to the current value.
    Adjust Mult (X) This will multiply the current value by X.
    REPT For boring operations: it specifies the number of holes.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
    SPCNG For boring operations: it specifies the spacing between holes.
 For a complete list see the System Parameters topic.

Adding an Object - Dim Object as New ObjectType

 You can create multiple objects as long as the objects have unique names.
 You can set the parameters for the new object(s) by specifying the ObjectName.Parameter

   (DE.DX).
 The parameter Visible will determine if the Part appears visually as well as on the cut list.

   (DE.Visible = True).
 It is common to link operations to other operations. For an operation to be valid it must be

   attached to a Part (not another operation). You can use the following statement to attach a new
   operation to the parent Part:

               NewObject.Owner = Owner
 This will effectively take the new operation and detach it from the operation and attach it to the

   Part.

Additional Functions

 Imp(X) Divides X by 25.4. Converts a metric value to imperial.
 Xmm establishes that you are defining a Metric value. 300mm
 Xin establishes that you are defining an Imperial value. 12in
 ? This is a wild card that can be used in any name to represent one character. B??D would

   match B24D and B18D but not B9D.
 * This is a wild card that can be used in any name to represent any number of characters. B*D

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
   would match B24D and B18D and B9D. However N*BORE would not match with
   NoooBoooBORE. When the program encounters an * it searches for the next character B in the
   rest of the string. When a match is found it performs the string comparison. In this case BORE =
   BoooBORE.

 Multiple wild cards can be used in any string: (W*3?D*BB)

 _M: Material Information. This parameter can be used to identify the current material
   information of any Part. Use _M:DZ to obtain the material thickness. Use _M:MatID to get the
   materials internal ID number. Use _M:SchID to get the current material schedule ID for a
   Part. The following would be valid syntax:

    _m:matid

    tr._m:schedid

    face.mr@2._m:dz

    cab.face.mr@2._m:matid

UCS Sample #2 Modify Manually Added Part

 In this example we will demonstrate some things to watch out for with advanced UCS. We will
   illustrate a system limitation imposed on UCS and how to work around the system.

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
UCSMOD Parameter

 UCS only applies to System Parts, unless you tell it to.
 Any New Part you add to an Object must have the UCSMOD = 1 Parameter added to it so the

   UCS will recognize the Part.

Example

 Add UCS that adjusts the Y position of all Top Stretchers
 Note that the Top Stretcher we have added doesn't change
 Add a UCSMOD = 1 Parameter to the Top Stretcher.
 Note: The Part is modified with every rebuild.
 This method is a valid method if you are not Adjusting the Part.
The parameter UCSMOD is used to add UCS control to Parts that have been manually added to
an object. Setting UCSMOD = 1 will allow you to make changes to the manually added Part via
UCS. The UCSMOD parameter will not work when the Part has been added by a UCS itself.
However, if you add a Part via a UCS, you should just size it correctly in that UCS.

UCS Sample #3 Modify Hinge Holes

 This example will demonstrate a modification to a CNC operation.
 It will move and rotate the holes for a base plate/hinge for the new Blum concealed base plate.
 The UCS must account for the differences in the Left end, Right end, & Partition.

         ;Preps Baseplate Holes For New Blum Concealed Base plates
          For Each HPBORE Linebore ;Hinge Plate Boring Holes
            Y Adjust Add imp(16) ;Move the Hinge Holes Up 16mm
            AZ = 90 ;Rotate the direction of the holes 90 degrees
            If X < imp(64) Then ;On Right End or Partitions
              AZ = -90 ;Reverse the Rotation
            End If

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
UCS Sample #4 Delete CNC Holes for Nailers

 This example originates from a customer who wanted CNC instructions for his Stretchers but
   not his nailers. Currently CABINET VISION assumes that if you have CNC for the Stretchers
   you will also have CNC for nailers.

 This example will demonstrate how to place a broad filter in the For Each line and place
   conditions on the parents name.

 Refer to the UCS constants for Operation Names.

         ;Deletes Construction Boring For Nailers
          For Each *HBORE Linebore
            If :Name == 'NA' Then ;If the parent is a nailer
              QTY = 0 ;Set the quantity of the operations to 0
            End If

UCS Sample #5 Add Light Rail To Uppers

         ;Links Bottom Rail to Bottom of Upper Assembly with Bottom Scribe
         For Each BO Part

          If Cab.Class == ASM_CLASS_UPPER Then
            If CAB.SCB > 0 Then ;If Assembly has bottom scribe > 0
              ;Initialize Variables with a default value
              LendThick = 0
              RendThick = 0
              ;These Values are only set if Unfinished Ends Exists
              If LEND = 2 Then
                LendThick = CAB.CASE.LU.DZ
              End If
              If REND = 2 Then
                RendThick = CAB.CASE.RU.DZ
              End If
              Dim BR as New Part
              BR.Visible = True
              BR.DX = CAB.SCB
              BR.DY = :DY + LendThick + RendThick
              BR.X = DZ
              BR.Y = 0 - LendThick
              BR.Z = :DZ
              BR.AX = 0
              BR.AY = -90
              BR.AZ = 0
            End If

          End If

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
UCS Sample #6 Add Additional Line of Vertical Boring Holes

 This standard links a set of line bore holes to an existing set of line boreholes.

 The standard has to use the Owner Keyword to work.

 Operations must be attached to Parts in order to be seen.

;Links Vertical Bore to Vertical  Bore
For Each LFVBORE Operation

 If Cab.DZ > 24 Then
   Dim VBORE as New Linebore
   VBORE.Owner = Owner
   VBORE.Visible = True
   VBORE.DX = :DX
   VBORE.DY = :DY
   VBORE.DY = :DZ
   VBORE.X = (::DX / 2) - :x
   VBORE.Y = 0
   VBORE.Z = 0
   VBORE.AX = :AX
   VBORE.AY = :AY
   VBORE.AZ = :AZ
   VBORE.REPT = :REPT
   VBORE.SPCNG = :SPCNG

 End If

Functions and Operators

Supported Operators and Mathematical Functions Computation Operations

Operators may be binary or unary. Binary operators have two operands such as in A * B. A and
B are the two operands in that expression. A unary operator has only one operand such as in !B.
In that expression, the (!) is a unary operator (meaning Boolean Not), because it has only one
operand (B).

(-) - Unary Minus

       Example: -X

(-) - Binary Minus

       Example: X - Y = Z

(+) - Unary Plus

                         © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
       Example: +X
(+) - Binary Plus

       Example: X + Y = Z
(*) - Multiplication

       Example: X = X * 2Y
(/) - Division

       Example: X = DX/2
(%) - Modulus

       Example: X = Y % Z
(^) - Exponential

       Example: X = Y ^ Z (Raises Y to the power of Z)

Comparison Operators

Comparison Operators return a Boolean Value (True or False) depending on the comparison
being made. For example, the expression 1 == 2 would return False.
(!) - Logical NOT

       Example: !a
(<) - Less Than

       Example: X < Y
(>) - Greater Than

       Example: Y > X
(<=) - Less Than or Equal To

       Example: X <= Y
(>=) - Greater Than or Equal To

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
       Example: Y >= X
(==) - Equivalence

       Example X == 1 (Must be used in Object Tree IF statements)
(!=) - Inequality

       Example: X != Y
(&) - Logical And

       Example; X & Y
(|) - Logical OR

       Example: X | Y

Checking for Null Values or a Parameters Existence

(null) - Null
       Example: If DX == null Then
                      DoSomething
                      End If

Assignment Operators

An assignment operator sets or re-sets the value assigned to a variable.
Valid assignment operators in CABINET VISION are:
(=) - Equals

       Example: X = 2 + 2; In this example, the variable (X) is assigned the value 2 + 2.
(:=) - Compute Now

       Example: X := 2 + 2; In this example, the variable (X) is assigned the value 4. This
       assignment operator varies from the (=) assignment operator in that with (:=):
       1. The expression is evaluated in the current state of the program, and

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
       2. The variable is assigned the computed value, replacing the prior value of that variable.
(+=) - Adjust Add

       Example: DX += 2 (This adds 2 to the current DX value)
(-=) - Adjust Subtract

       Example: DX -= 2 (This subtracts 2 from the current DX value)
(*=) - Adjust Multiply

       Example: DX *= 2 (This multiplies the current DX value by 2)
(/=) - Adjust Divide

       Example: DX /= 2 (This divides the current DX value by 2)
Deleting a Parameter (Via UCS)
(Delete) - Delete

       Example: Delete DX (This will remove the DX Parameter from the Object)

The "This" Object

The "this" object is a substitute for what is in the For Each statement. The example below shows
the difference in using it:
;Not Using the THIS Object
For Each DWR_OPEN|DOR_OPEN Part

       If DWR_OPEN.DOR.S_DSLAB.DX > 5 Then
               Do Something

       End if
       If DOR_OPEN.DOR.S_DSLAB.DX > 5 Then

               Do The Same Something As Above
       End if

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
The code above when using the "this" object could be replaced with:
;Using the THIS Object
For Each DWR_OPEN|DOR_OPEN Part

       If this.DOR.S_DSLAB.DX > 5 Then
               Do It All

       End if

Define Value types in a UCS

You can define the following Value types via a UCS.
Currency <crncy>

       A system of money in general use in a particular country
Measurement <meas>

       The size, length, or amount of something, as established by measuring. Note: This is the
       default type used when no type is defined. When Measurement is the type the value will be
       converted between Imperial and Metric based on the current active unit of measurement.
Degrees <deg>
       A unit of measurement of angles, one three-hundred-and-sixtieth of the circumference of a
       circle.
Integer <int>
       A number that is not a fraction; a whole number.
Boolean <bool>
       A Boolean data type is a fundamental data type in computer science that represents two
       possible values: true (1) or false (0).
Decimal <dec>
       Defines exact numeric values.
Text <text>

                                                                     © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
You can also build strings of Text in CABINET VISION from the results of existing Parameters
or AutoText Values. Such as the three examples below:

NAME = w{DX}h{DY}d{DZ}

PARTMAT = {material}

COMMENT = {name} ({job.name})

Style <style>

There are three possible settings for the <style> value:

0 = Value

       Values act as previous Parameter definitions, only displayed in the Object Tree and hard set
by the UCS.

1 = Attribute

       Attributes act as triggers that can be user prompted from the sidebar for the Object or via
Job/Room Parameters tabs. Use <desc> (below) to set the prompt description.

2 = Note

       Notes are a user defined Note which will be displayed on the Notes pages for the Object and
available as CAD text look-ups. The text entered for Notes are default values which can be edited
from the prompt. Use <desc> (below) to set the prompt description.

Description <desc>

Description allows you to display a user prompt for Attribute and Note Parameters.

Below is a sample UCS showing how to format utilizing these functions:

;Assigning Value Types in a UCS

If U_DWStrip == null then                 ;Checks to see if the U_DWStrip already

False) with a default of False

                                 © 2026 Hexagon AB and/or its subsidiaries.
Cabinet

End If

If Cab.U_DWStrip == 1 Then          ;Checks to see if the User said Yes to Add
Dishwasher Strip Question

Dim BOARD as New Part

BOARD.X<meas> = 0                   ;meas = Measurement

BOARD.Y<meas> = Cab.DY              ;meas = Measurement

BOARD.Z<meas> = 0                   ;meas = Measurement

BOARD.DX<meas> = 1.75               ;meas = Measurement

BOARD.DY<meas> = 24                 ;meas = Measurement

BOARD.AX<deg> = 0                   ;deg = Degrees

BOARD.AY<deg> = 0                   ;deg = Degrees

BOARD.AZ<deg> = -90                 ;deg = Degrees

BOARD.QTY<int> = 3                  ;int = Integer

BOARD.WEIGHT<dec> = 23.25           ;dec = Decimal

 NOTE<text> = 'Extra Board for Mounting Dishwasher Included'                  ;defines the text contained in
NOTE

 NOTE<style> = 2                                                              ;sets the Parameter NOTE
as a Note on the CAB in For Each

You can also define a list of values for a user to select from. See the Parameters topic for more
information.

While CAB.INTERIOR.{_NAME}@{_COUNT}.DX > 0 Do

        Exit
    End If
    _COUNT += 1
End While
